children.topic: 1. The branches of accounting at a glance
children.note: Accounting is one big family with many branches. Each branch serves a different person and answers a different question. This map gives you the whole family in one view before you study any branch in depth.
Cost accounting works out what each product, job or service costs, so a business can price well, cut waste and plan. This map gives the big picture and points you to the CPA maps for depth.

Tax accounting is the branch that works out how much tax a person or business owes, keeps the records to prove it, and files it with the tax authority (in Kenya, KRA). This map is a big-picture tour; the CPA tax papers go into the detail.

Internal audit is a team inside an organisation that checks, on behalf of the board, whether risks are being managed and controls really work. This map gives a beginner's overview; the CPA auditing papers go deeper.

Forensic accounting is accounting used to find, prove and explain fraud and money disputes. This map covers why people cheat, the common tricks, the warning signs, how an investigation runs and how a business protects itself.

How governments, counties and public bodies keep and report the accounts for public money. The aim is not profit but showing citizens that money was raised and spent as the law and the budget allowed.
How businesses count their effect on nature: environmental costs, greenhouse gas emissions (scopes 1, 2, 3) and carbon credits, with simple worked examples and Kenyan context.

Social and impact accounting measures and reports the good and harm an organisation does to people and the planet, not just its profit. You will learn the results chain, SROI with a KES example, the triple bottom line, GRI and impact investing.
How finance works under Islamic rules: no interest, real assets, shared risk. You learn the main contracts, how to record them in KES, zakat basics and the Kenyan scene.

How a business captures, stores and reports its money data, from paper books to ERP systems. Covers the parts of an AIS, transaction cycles, coding, data flow, controls and Kenyan links like eTIMS and M-Pesa.

children.note: How Kenyan SACCOs and co-operatives keep their books: members' deposits and shares, loans and loss provisions, rebates and dividends, reserves and the regulators. Uses an invented SACCO for every example.
How banks and microfinance institutions keep their books. Their 'stock' is money: deposits they owe and loans they are owed. Examples use invented banks and KES figures; this is a general guide only.
How insurers keep their books: premiums earned over time, claims and reserves, reinsurance and agent commission, and IFRS 17 in plain words. A general guide with an invented insurer and figures.

How farms and agribusinesses keep their books: simple records for a small farm, cost per litre or per bag, the IAS 41 rules for living animals and plants, cooperatives like KTDA and dairy co-ops, and grants. All farm names and figures are invented.
How private hospitals and clinics keep their books: income by department, many payers, insurer and SHA claims, drug stock, costly machines and patient privacy. Uses an invented clinic and figures.

nodeData.topic: The branches of accounting at a glance
nodeData.note: Accounting is one big family with many branches. Each branch serves a different person and answers a different question. This map gives you the whole family in one view before you study any branch in depth.

children.topic: 1. What accounting is, and why branches
children.note: Start here: what accounting does and why it splits into branches.
Accounting records what an organisation does with money and reports it to the people who need to know, such as owners, lenders, managers and the government.

manas.q: What is accounting?

children.note: Bookkeeping is the daily recording of transactions, usually by double entry. Every branch of accounting is built on these records.

manas.q: What is bookkeeping?

children.note: Different people ask different questions. An owner asks "did we make a profit?", KRA asks "how much tax?", a manager asks "what does one unit cost?". Each question grew its own branch.
The branches most accountants use every day: telling outsiders how the business did, and helping managers run it.
Records transactions and prepares financial statements for people outside the business, following set rules (IFRS, or IFRS for SMEs for smaller Kenyan entities).

manas.q: What is financial accounting?

children.topic: Who uses it, and the question
children.note: Owners, shareholders, banks, suppliers and regulators. It answers: how did the business perform, and what does it own and owe?
A company listed on the Nairobi Securities Exchange publishes an audited annual report with a statement of profit or loss and a statement of financial position.
Basics at Foundation level, then full IFRS reporting (CA23 Financial Reporting).
Prepares information for managers inside the business to plan, control and decide. No outside rulebook; the format is whatever helps the manager.

manas.q: What is management accounting?

children.topic: Who uses it, and the question
children.note: Managers and directors. It answers: what should we do next, and are we on plan?
A matatu SACCO compares fuel cost per route each month and drops a route that loses money.
Budgets, variances and decisions (CA25 Management Accounting).
Records, groups and shares out costs so the business knows what each product, job or service really costs. It mainly feeds management accounting.

manas.q: What is cost accounting?

children.topic: Who uses it, and the question
children.note: Production managers and pricing teams. It answers: what does one unit cost, and is our price high enough?
A Nakuru bakery works out the cost of one loaf: flour, labour, gas and a share of rent.
Costing methods and overheads (CA25 Management Accounting).
Branches that test whether the numbers are true, honest and taxed correctly.
Works out tax under the tax law, which often differs from accounting rules, and prepares returns.

manas.q: What is tax accounting?

children.topic: Who uses it, and the question
children.note: Business owners, tax advisers and the Kenya Revenue Authority. It answers: how much tax is due, and when?
A duka owner files VAT and income tax returns on KRA iTax. Rates change, so check the current KRA rate.
Income tax, VAT and public finance (CA26 Public Finance and Taxation).
An independent auditor examines the financial statements and gives an opinion on whether they are fairly stated.

manas.q: What is an external audit?

children.topic: Who uses it, and the question
children.note: Shareholders, lenders and regulators. It answers: can we trust these financial statements?
A registered audit firm audits a Kenyan SACCO and its report goes to members at the AGM.
Audit process, evidence and reports (CA24 Auditing and Assurance).
Staff (or hired helpers) who check, all year round, that controls work and policies are followed. They report to management and the audit committee.

manas.q: How does internal audit differ from external audit?

children.topic: Who uses it, and the question
children.note: Boards, audit committees and managers. It answers: are our controls working and are risks managed?
A SACCO internal auditor checks that every loan was approved by the right committee and matched to a guarantor.
Internal control and internal audit (CA24 Auditing and Assurance); a later topic here goes deeper.
Investigates suspected fraud or financial misconduct and produces evidence that can stand up in court.

manas.q: What is forensic accounting?

children.topic: Who uses it, and the question
children.note: Courts, police, boards, insurers and lawyers. It answers: did someone steal or lie, how, and how much?
A chain of shops finds M-Pesa float missing; a forensic accountant traces the till records and finds the gap.
Fraud and the auditor (CA24 Auditing and Assurance); a later topic here goes deeper.

children.topic: 4. Branches for public money and donors
children.note: Branches where the aim is accountability for money, not profit.
Accounting for national and county governments and state bodies. Kenyan public bodies use IPSAS-based rules issued by the Public Sector Accounting Standards Board.

manas.q: What is public sector accounting?

children.topic: Who uses it, and the question
children.note: Parliament, county assemblies, taxpayers and the Auditor-General. It answers: was public money spent as the budget allowed?
A county government reports what it spent on health against its approved budget, and the Office of the Auditor-General audits it.
Budgets and public finance (CA26 Public Finance and Taxation), then (CA34S4 Advanced Public Financial Management).
Charities, churches and NGOs keep separate funds for money given for a set purpose. The focus is accountability, not profit.

manas.q: What is fund accounting?

children.topic: Who uses it, and the question
children.note: Donors, trustees and members. It answers: was each gift used for the purpose it was given?
An NGO gets a grant only for borehole drilling in Kitui; it keeps a separate restricted fund and reports how every shilling was spent.
Ideas of fund control appear in (CA34S4 Advanced Public Financial Management); a later topic here covers the public sector.
Branches that grew from new needs: the planet, society, faith-based finance, computers and trust.
Measures environmental costs and impacts, in money and in physical units such as tonnes of greenhouse gas emitted.

manas.q: What is carbon (GHG) accounting?

children.topic: Who uses it, and the question
children.note: Investors, lenders, regulators and customers. It answers: what does our business do to the environment, and what does it cost us?
A Naivasha flower farm tracks water use and the emissions from flying flowers to Europe.
Sustainability reporting links to (CA23 Financial Reporting); a later topic here goes deeper.
Reports the social effects of an organisation: jobs, community, staff welfare, not just profit.

manas.q: What is social accounting?

children.topic: Who uses it, and the question
children.note: Communities, staff, investors and donors. It answers: what good or harm do we do to people?
A tea factory reports how many smallholder farmers it pays and its school support in the area.
A later topic in this section covers it.
Accounting for deals that follow Sharia, which bans interest (riba). Uses contracts such as murabaha (cost-plus sale) and ijara (leasing).

manas.q: What does Islamic finance prohibit?

children.topic: Who uses it, and the question
children.note: Islamic banks, their customers and Sharia boards. It answers: is this deal Sharia compliant and how do we report it?
A Kenyan bank offers Sharia-compliant car finance: it buys the car and sells it to the customer at an agreed mark-up.
A later topic in this section covers it.
The computer systems that collect, store and process accounting data and produce reports for every other branch.

manas.q: What is an accounting information system (AIS)?

children.topic: Who uses it, and the question
children.note: Accountants, managers, IT staff and auditors. It answers: is our data captured fully, accurately and safely?
A hospital pharmacy links its till, M-Pesa payments and stock records into one accounting package.
IT controls appear in (CA24 Auditing and Assurance); a later topic here goes deeper.

Someone who looks after money for another person (a trustee or executor) keeps accounts showing exactly what came in and went out. Example: an executor handling a deceased farmer's estate for the family.

manas.q: What is a fiduciary?

children.note: Works out pay, deductions and employer contributions every month and pays them on time. Example: a hotel paying staff and sending deductions to KRA; check current KRA rates.
The two biggest branches side by side. Exams love this comparison.
Financial accounting serves outsiders such as owners, banks and KRA. Management accounting serves managers inside the business.

manas.q: Who uses financial accounting vs management accounting?

children.note: Financial accounting must follow IFRS (or IFRS for SMEs) and company law. Management accounting has no required format.

manas.q: Must management accounts follow IFRS?

children.topic: Timing: past yearly vs future often
children.note: Financial accounts are mostly yearly (sometimes half-yearly) and look back. Management reports can be weekly or daily and often look forward with budgets.

children.topic: Detail: whole firm vs each part
children.note: Financial statements summarise the whole entity. Management reports drill down to each product, branch, route or shift.
Financial accounts are in shillings. Management reports also use litres, hours, customers served or waste levels.
Financial statements of companies are usually audited by law. Management reports are not audited.
A Nakuru dairy buys a milk cooler for KES 1,200,000 on credit. See how four branches look at the same event.
The dairy receives a KES 1,200,000 milk cooler from a supplier and will pay in 60 days. Assume it lasts 8 years with no value at the end.
Dr Equipment (cooler) KES 1,200,000 / Cr Trade payables KES 1,200,000. Debits 1,200,000 = credits 1,200,000, so it balances.
Straight line: 1,200,000 ÷ 8 years = KES 150,000 a year. Dr Depreciation expense 150,000 / Cr Accumulated depreciation 150,000.
Assets go up 1,200,000 and liabilities go up 1,200,000, so the balance sheet still balances. After year 1 the cooler shows at 1,050,000.
The dairy chills 600,000 litres a year. Cooler cost per litre = 150,000 ÷ 600,000 = KES 0.25 per litre.
If milk used to cost KES 40.00 a litre to handle, it now costs 40.25. The manager asks: does cooling cut spoilage by more than 25 cents a litre?
For tax, the KES 150,000 depreciation is added back and a capital allowance (wear and tear deduction) is claimed under the Income Tax Act. Check the current KRA rate for this class of machine.
Depreciation and capital allowance usually differ each year. The timing gap creates deferred tax under IAS 12 Income Taxes.
The auditor checks that the cooler exists, belongs to the dairy, cost KES 1,200,000 and the payable is complete.
Supplier invoice and delivery note for the amount and date; supplier statement to confirm the payable.
Physically inspect the cooler on site and match its serial number to the fixed asset register.
Recalculate the depreciation of 150,000 and check the useful life of 8 years is reasonable.
Mix-ups that cost marks.
Bookkeeping records; accounting also summarises, analyses and reports. Do not use the words as if they mean the same.
Cost accounting is one tool inside management accounting. Management accounting is wider: budgets, decisions, performance.
The external auditor gives an opinion to shareholders and must be independent. The internal auditor serves management and checks controls.
An audit gives reasonable assurance on the whole set of accounts. A forensic review digs deep into one suspected wrong for legal use.
Tax law has its own rules, so taxable profit is rarely equal to accounting profit. Never use depreciation as a tax deduction.

children.topic: Q1: Four differences, financial vs management
children.note: Give four differences between financial and management accounting.
Users (outside vs inside); rules (IFRS required vs none); timing (yearly and past vs frequent and future); detail (whole entity vs each part).

children.topic: Q2: Which branch checks SACCO loans?
children.note: A SACCO board wants someone on staff to check all year that loans follow policy. Name the branch.
Internal audit: it is ongoing, reports to the board or audit committee, and tests controls such as loan approvals.
A KES 900,000 pasteuriser lasts 6 years, no value at the end, and handles 500,000 litres a year. Find the cost per litre.

children.note: A duka buys a delivery van for KES 2,400,000 on credit. Write the journal.
Dr Motor vehicles KES 2,400,000 / Cr Trade payables KES 2,400,000. Debits equal credits.

nodeData.note: Cost accounting works out what each product, job or service costs, so a business can price well, cut waste and plan. This map gives the big picture and points you to the CPA maps for depth.

children.note: Cost accounting finds out what each product, job or service really costs to make or deliver. Owners use the answer to set prices, cut waste and plan.
Cost accounting records, sorts and studies a business's costs so managers know the cost of each thing it makes or each service it gives.

manas.q: What is cost accounting?

children.note: If you do not know your cost, you cannot know your profit. A price set below cost loses money on every sale, however busy the shop looks.
Cost figures help managers set selling prices, spot waste, compare actual spending with plans, and decide what to make more of or stop.

manas.q: Name three uses of cost accounting.

children.note: Its reports go to owners and managers, not to the public. They can be daily, by product, by branch, in any shape that helps a decision.
It grew in the Industrial Revolution, when factories became big and owners needed a careful way to measure and share out their costs.
In a big firm, cost accountants and management accountants. In a small duka or bakery, often the owner or a part-time bookkeeper with a simple spreadsheet.
Jobs include cost accountant, cost clerk, management accountant, financial analyst and budget officer, in factories, farms, hospitals and NGOs. CPA (KASNEB) is the usual Kenyan route.
Before any method, learn the three basic ideas: what you cost (cost unit), where the cost arises (cost centre), and what the cost is made of (elements).

children.topic: Cost unit: the thing you cost
children.note: A cost unit is one item or measure you want the cost of: a loaf, a gate, a patient visit, a passenger-km, a stem of roses.

manas.q: What is a cost unit?

children.note: A cost centre is a department or activity where costs are collected, such as the bakery oven room, the clinic lab or the farm packhouse.

manas.q: What is a cost centre?

children.note: A profit centre is a part of the business that earns income as well as spending, so its manager answers for profit, like one matatu or one branch.

manas.q: How is a profit centre different from a cost centre?

children.note: Every cost is materials, labour or other expenses. Each one can be direct (traced to the unit) or indirect (shared out, called overheads).

manas.q: What are the three elements of cost?

children.note: Things used up to make the product, such as flour and sugar in bread or steel in a gate.
Pay for people's work, such as the baker's wages or the welder's hourly pay.
Other costs, such as electricity, rent, fuel, hire of a special machine or insurance.
A direct cost can be traced straight to one cost unit, like the flour in a loaf or the steel in one customer's gate.

manas.q: What is a direct cost?

children.note: An indirect cost is shared by many units and cannot be traced to one, like factory rent or the supervisor's salary.

manas.q: What are overheads?

children.note: Prime cost = direct materials + direct labour + direct expenses. It is the cost before any overheads are added.

manas.q: What is the formula for prime cost?

children.note: Total cost = prime cost + overheads (production, admin, selling). Divide by units made to get cost per unit.

manas.q: How do you get total cost per unit?

children.note: Some costs stay the same when output changes (rent: fixed); others rise with output (flour: variable). The CA25 map on cost behaviour goes deeper.
The method depends on what the business makes: one-off jobs, batches, a flowing process, long contracts, or a service.
Costs are collected for each separate customer order. Used by welders, printers, garages and tailors where every job is different.

manas.q: When is job costing used?

children.note: A Kamukunji welder records the steel, hours and a share of workshop costs for each gate he makes to order.
A batch of identical items is costed as one job, then the batch cost is divided by the number of items.

manas.q: What is batch costing?

children.note: A bakery costs one tray-run of 200 cupcakes, then divides by 200 to get the cost of one cake.
Used when the same product flows through stages non-stop. Costs of a period are averaged over all units produced.

manas.q: When is process costing used?

children.note: A dairy or juice factory adds up a month's costs and divides by the litres produced.
Some loss is expected in a process (spills, evaporation). Its cost is spread over the good units left.
A form of job costing for big, long jobs that last months or years, such as building a school or a road.

manas.q: What is contract costing?

children.note: Long contracts recognise revenue and profit as the work progresses, in line with IFRS 15 Revenue from Contracts with Customers.
Used where a business sells a service, not goods. The cost unit is a measure of service like a passenger-km, a patient-day or a room-night.

manas.q: What is service costing and give a cost unit?

children.note: Matatu: cost per passenger-km. Clinic: cost per patient visit. Hotel: cost per room-night. School: cost per pupil per term.
Ask: is each order different (job), made in groups (batch), flowing non-stop (process), huge and long (contract), or a service (service costing)?
Three related branches. Financial accounting reports to outsiders; cost accounting finds costs; management accounting uses costs and more to help decide.
Prepares the yearly statements for owners, banks, KRA and the public, following IFRS or IFRS for SMEs.

manas.q: Who are financial accounts mainly for?

children.note: Works out the cost of products, jobs and services. It is mostly internal and has no set legal format.
The wider branch: uses cost data plus budgets and forecasts to help managers plan and decide. Cost accounting sits inside it.

manas.q: How does cost accounting relate to management accounting?

children.note: Financial accounts look back at what happened. Cost and management accounts also look forward: budgets, quotes and what-if choices.
Financial accounts must follow standards. Cost reports only need to be useful and correct, so each business can design its own.
Inventory in the financial statements is valued at cost, so the cost figures from costing feed straight into the balance sheet (IAS 2 Inventories).
Real-looking Kenyan numbers, each one checked so it adds up.
1,000 loaves: materials KES 18,000 + labour KES 8,000 = prime cost KES 26,000. Add overheads KES 6,000 = total KES 32,000, so KES 32 per loaf.
Selling price KES 50 − cost KES 32 = KES 18 profit per loaf, or KES 18,000 on 1,000 loaves.
Steel KES 14,500 + labour 10 hrs × KES 400 = KES 4,000 + overhead 10 hrs × KES 150 = KES 1,500. Job cost KES 20,000.
KES 20,000 × 1.25 = KES 25,000 price, giving KES 5,000 profit on the job.
Steel issued to the job: Dr Work in progress KES 14,500 / Cr Raw materials inventory KES 14,500. Both sides equal.
Materials KES 12,000 + labour KES 6,000 + power KES 4,000 + other overheads KES 8,000 = KES 30,000. ÷ 200 = KES 150 per cake.
Month: fruit KES 400,000 + labour KES 120,000 + overheads KES 80,000 = KES 600,000 for 10,000 litres = KES 60 per litre.
Month: fuel 120,000 + crew 60,000 + insurance 15,000 + repairs 20,000 + depreciation 25,000 = KES 240,000.
4 trips × 30 km × 25 days = 3,000 km. KES 240,000 ÷ 3,000 = KES 80 per km.
Average 16 passengers: 3,000 × 16 = 48,000 passenger-km. KES 240,000 ÷ 48,000 = KES 5 per passenger-km.
A small clinic spends KES 450,000 a month and sees 1,500 patients, so each visit costs KES 300 on average.
A Naivasha rose farm spends KES 3,600,000 in a month and cuts 1,200,000 stems: KES 3 per stem before freight.
Contract price KES 10,000,000; expected total cost KES 8,000,000. Expected profit KES 2,000,000, which is 20% of the price.
Traps that catch beginners and exam candidates.
Pricing on materials alone. Rent, power and supervision must be added, or every sale secretly loses money.
The cost unit is what you cost (a loaf); the cost centre is where costs gather (the oven room).
Using process costing for one-off orders, or job costing for a non-stop dairy line, gives misleading costs.
Cost is what you spend; price is what the customer pays. Profit is the gap between them.
Divide total cost by good units produced, not by units sold or units started.

nodeData.note: Tax accounting is the branch that works out how much tax a person or business owes, keeps the records to prove it, and files it with the tax authority (in Kenya, KRA). This map is a big-picture tour; the CPA tax papers go into the detail.

children.note: Start here: what the branch does and why every business needs it.
Tax accounting means measuring income and costs the way the tax law says, so the right tax is paid on time. Financial accounting follows accounting standards; tax accounting follows the tax laws.

manas.q: What is tax accounting?

children.note: Getting tax wrong costs money: penalties, interest and stress. Getting it right keeps the business legal and lets it plan its cash.
The Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA) is the government agency that assesses and collects taxes and customs duties in Kenya. Other countries have their own (for example HMRC in the UK).

manas.q: Who collects taxes in Kenya?

children.topic: Two sets of rules, one business
children.note: The same duka keeps one set of records but reads them two ways: the accounting rules give 'accounting profit', the tax rules give 'taxable profit'.

children.topic: Where it sits among the branches
children.note: Financial accounting reports to owners, cost accounting helps managers, tax accounting deals with the government. They all use the same books.
The big idea of the branch: the profit in the accounts is not always the profit that is taxed.
Accounting profit is the profit in the income statement, worked out using accounting standards (IFRS or IFRS for SMEs).

manas.q: What is accounting profit?

children.note: Taxable profit is the profit the tax law charges tax on. You get it by adjusting accounting profit for items the tax law treats differently.

manas.q: What is taxable profit?

children.note: Some costs are in the accounts but the tax law does not let you deduct them, for example fines, the owner's private spending, or depreciation. You add them back to accounting profit.

manas.q: What is an add-back in a tax computation?

children.note: Some income is in the accounts but is not taxed (or is taxed separately), so you take it out of the computation. Which items qualify depends on the current law.

manas.q: Why might some income be deducted in a tax computation?

children.note: Depreciation is the accountant's own estimate of an asset wearing out. Tax law usually ignores it and gives its own deduction instead, called capital allowances.

manas.q: Why is depreciation added back for tax?

children.note: Capital allowances are the tax law's version of depreciation: fixed deductions for buying business assets like machines, vans or buildings. The rates are set in law, so check the current KRA rules.

manas.q: What are capital allowances?

children.note: Start with accounting profit, add disallowed costs, take away non-taxable income and capital allowances, and you reach taxable profit. Then apply the tax rate.

manas.q: What is the basic layout of a tax computation?

children.note: Some differences never reverse (a fine is never deductible). Others only change WHEN a cost is deducted, like capital allowances vs depreciation. Timing differences lead to deferred tax.
Taxes come in two big families. Knowing which family a tax is in tells you who really bears it.
A direct tax is charged on a person's or company's own income or profit, and they bear it themselves. Examples: income tax, PAYE on salaries, corporation tax.

manas.q: What is a direct tax?

children.note: An indirect tax is added to the price of goods or services. The business collects it and passes it to KRA, but the final customer really pays it. Examples: VAT, excise duty, customs duty.

manas.q: What is an indirect tax?

children.note: PAYE is income tax taken from employees' salaries by the employer each month and paid to KRA. The bands change, so always check the current KRA rates.

manas.q: What is PAYE?

children.note: Value Added Tax is charged at each step of selling. A registered business charges VAT on sales (output VAT), claims back VAT on purchases (input VAT), and pays the difference.

manas.q: How does VAT work in simple terms?

children.note: Excise duty falls on chosen goods such as drinks, fuel and airtime. Customs duty falls on goods brought into the country. Both are collected by KRA.
Some payments (for example certain fees, rent or dividends) have tax taken off by the payer at source and sent to KRA. The receiver may later set it against their own tax.
Tax work is done in three main places. Each one sees the same law from a different side.
Works inside one company or hospital. Prepares monthly VAT and PAYE, the yearly return, and keeps the tax records tidy for audits.
Works in a firm and serves many clients: filing returns, giving tax planning advice, and handling disputes with KRA. Big audit firms and small local practices both do this.
Work for the government side: checking returns, running audits, collecting arrears and helping taxpayers use iTax and eTIMS.
Many duka and matatu owners do their own simple returns. They still need good records and a basic idea of what is taxable.
Run monthly payroll and work out deductions such as PAYE and other statutory deductions, then pay them over on time.

children.topic: 5. The yearly compliance cycle in Kenya
children.note: Being 'tax compliant' is a routine: keep records, issue proper invoices, file returns, pay on time. Exact deadlines change, so always check the current KRA dates.
Keep sales, purchase invoices, receipts, bank and M-Pesa statements, payroll and asset records. The law requires records to be kept for several years.

manas.q: What is the first step of tax compliance?

children.note: eTIMS is KRA's electronic Tax Invoice Management System. Businesses issue invoices through it so KRA can see each sale. KRA may not accept costs that are not backed by a valid electronic invoice.

manas.q: What is eTIMS?

children.note: Some taxes are reported every month, for example PAYE and VAT for registered businesses. Check the current KRA due date for each.

manas.q: Which taxes are usually filed monthly?

children.topic: Step 4: The yearly income tax return
children.note: Once a year, individuals and companies file an income tax return on iTax showing income, allowances and tax due. Check the current KRA deadline.

manas.q: What is filed once a year on iTax?

children.note: iTax is KRA's online portal where taxpayers register for a PIN, file returns, pay tax and download certificates.

manas.q: What is iTax?

children.note: Filing is not paying. Tax is paid through the bank or mobile money using a payment slip from iTax. Late payment usually brings penalties and interest.

children.topic: Step 6: Keep proof and answer KRA
children.note: Save acknowledgement receipts and payment slips. If KRA asks questions or starts an audit, the records are your defence.
A document from KRA showing a taxpayer is up to date. Businesses often need it to win tenders or renew licences.
Three words that sound alike but sit in very different places: fine, grey and illegal.
Arranging your affairs within the law and its intention to pay the right tax, for example claiming every allowance you are entitled to or timing an asset purchase.

manas.q: What is tax planning?

children.note: Using the letter of the law in ways it was not meant for, to cut tax. It may be legal, but tax authorities can challenge it under anti-avoidance rules and it can harm reputation.

manas.q: What is tax avoidance?

children.note: Deliberately paying less than you owe by lying or hiding, for example not recording cash sales or inventing expenses. It is illegal and can lead to fines and prison.

manas.q: What is tax evasion?

children.note: Ask: is it within the law, and does it follow what the law intended? Yes and yes = planning. Legal but against the spirit = avoidance. Hiding or lying = evasion.
Professional accountants must never help with evasion. ICPAK's code of ethics expects honesty and integrity even under client pressure.
Deferred tax smooths out timing differences between the accounts and the tax rules, so the tax charge matches the profit shown.
Current tax is the tax actually payable to KRA for this year, worked out from taxable profit.

manas.q: What is current tax?

children.note: Deferred tax is tax that will be paid (or saved) in future years because of timing differences between accounting and tax rules. It is shown as a liability or an asset.

manas.q: What is deferred tax?

children.note: The carrying amount is what an asset is worth in the accounts; the tax base is what it is worth for tax. The gap between them is the temporary difference.

manas.q: What is a temporary difference?

children.note: If tax relief came early (big capital allowances), more tax is due later: a deferred tax liability. If tax relief comes later (for example tax losses to use), you get a deferred tax asset.
IAS 12 is the accounting standard for income taxes, covering both current and deferred tax. IFRS for SMEs has its own simpler section on income tax.

manas.q: Which standard covers deferred tax?

children.note: Real numbers in KES. The tax rates used here are made up for practice only; always check the current KRA rate.

children.topic: Example 1: from accounting to taxable profit
children.note: Mama Wanjiku Traders Ltd shows accounting profit of KES 2,000,000. Let's adjust it.
Accounting profit KES 2,000,000. Depreciation charged KES 300,000. A traffic fine KES 50,000. Owner's private spending KES 70,000. Capital allowances KES 400,000.
Assume a 30% rate for this example only. KES 2,020,000 × 30% = KES 606,000 tax.
Dr Income tax expense KES 606,000 / Cr Tax payable KES 606,000. When paid: Dr Tax payable KES 606,000 / Cr Bank KES 606,000.
A duka buys stock for KES 100,000 and sells it for KES 150,000 (both before VAT). Assume a 10% VAT rate for this example only (not the real rate).
VAT paid on purchases: 10% × 100,000 = KES 10,000. VAT charged on sales: 10% × 150,000 = KES 15,000.
15,000 − 10,000 = KES 5,000 paid to KRA. The duka only passes the tax through; its customers carried it.

children.topic: Example 3: deferred tax on a machine
children.note: A clinic buys a machine for KES 1,200,000. The accounts depreciate it over 4 years. Assume the tax law gives 100% allowance in year 1 and a 30% tax rate (made up for this example only).
Depreciation 1,200,000 ÷ 4 = KES 300,000, so carrying amount = KES 900,000. Full allowance given, so tax base = KES 0.
900,000 − 0 = KES 900,000. Tax relief came early, so more tax will be due later.
900,000 × 30% = KES 270,000. Dr Deferred tax expense KES 270,000 / Cr Deferred tax liability KES 270,000.
Where beginners and exam candidates most often lose marks.
Depreciation is in the accounts but not allowed for tax. Add it back, then deduct capital allowances instead.
Avoidance can be legal; evasion is a crime. Read the question for words like 'hid', 'did not record' or 'false'.

children.topic: Thinking VAT is the business's cost
children.note: For a registered business, VAT is collected for KRA. The profit is measured without the VAT.
Tax rates and bands change, often each Finance Act. Use the rate the exam gives, and in practice check the current KRA rate.
A nil or full return does not clear the tax due. Penalties and interest run until payment is made.
Try each one, then open the bubbles for the steps. Rates are made up for practice.

children.topic: Q1: Compute taxable profit and tax
children.note: Accounting profit KES 800,000; depreciation KES 120,000; fine KES 30,000; capital allowances KES 150,000. Assume a 25% rate.
Classify: PAYE, VAT, corporation tax, excise duty.
Direct: PAYE and corporation tax (charged on your own income). Indirect: VAT and excise duty (added to prices, carried by the buyer).
(a) A trader leaves cash sales out of the books. (b) A company buys a machine before year end to claim the allowance this year.
(a) is evasion, because income is hidden. (b) is tax planning, because it uses an allowance the law intends to give.
An asset's carrying amount is KES 500,000 and its tax base is KES 350,000. Assume a 30% rate.
Temporary difference 500,000 − 350,000 = KES 150,000. Deferred tax liability = 150,000 × 30% = KES 45,000.

nodeData.note: Internal audit is a team inside an organisation that checks, on behalf of the board, whether risks are being managed and controls really work. This map gives a beginner's overview; the CPA auditing papers go deeper.

children.note: Start here: who internal auditors are, what they do and how they differ from the external auditors.
Internal auditors are staff (or hired experts) who look at how the organisation is run and say honestly what works and what does not. They then suggest improvements.

manas.q: What is internal audit, in one sentence?

children.note: Assurance work means giving the board and managers an objective opinion on whether risks are controlled. Example: "Is the pharmacy stock safe from theft?"

manas.q: What is assurance work in internal audit?

children.note: Consulting work means giving advice when managers ask, for example on designing controls for a new M-Pesa payment system. The auditor advises but does not take the decision.

manas.q: What is consulting work in internal audit?

children.note: Three big areas: how the organisation is governed, how it manages risk, and whether its controls work. Controls cover operations, reports and obeying laws.
Internal audit can review anything risky: IT systems, procurement, safety, patient records handling, fleet fuel use. Finance is only one area.

children.topic: Not the people who do the work
children.note: Internal auditors check processes; they do not run them. If they ran them, they would end up checking their own work.

manas.q: Why should internal auditors not run the processes they audit?

children.note: The two often get mixed up. Here are the main differences.
Internal audit serves the board and management. External auditors report to the shareholders (owners).

manas.q: To whom does internal audit report, and to whom does external audit report?

children.note: External audit gives one opinion: do the financial statements give a true and fair view? Internal audit gives many reports on risks, controls and efficiency.

manas.q: What opinion does an external auditor give?

children.note: External audit happens mainly once a year. Internal audit works all year round under a yearly plan.
External audit of companies is required by law (Companies Act 2015 in Kenya). Internal audit is a choice for most private firms, but required for public bodies.
Yes. External auditors may use some internal audit work after judging it reliable, which saves time and fees.
Internal audit is only useful if it can speak freely. This branch covers who it reports to and where it sits.
If the finance manager can stop a bad report, the board never hears the truth. Independence lets auditors report problems without fear.

manas.q: Why does internal audit need independence?

children.note: The head of internal audit reports on audit matters to the audit committee of the board. Day-to-day admin (leave, office) can go to the CEO.

manas.q: What is the 'dual reporting line' of the head of internal audit?

children.note: A small group of board members, ideally independent, who oversee financial reporting, internal and external audit and risk. They approve the audit plan.
A short written document, approved by the board, that sets internal audit's purpose, powers (e.g. access to all records) and reporting lines.

manas.q: What is an internal audit charter?

children.note: Each auditor must be fair and not biased. Example: someone who worked in stores last year should not audit stores this year.
The IIA's model shows how roles in an organisation fit together to manage risk. Described here in our own words.
Sits above the lines. It sets direction, accepts responsibility for oversight and receives reports from management and internal audit.

children.topic: First line: managers who run things
children.note: The people who deliver the service own the risks day to day, e.g. the pharmacy in-charge who keeps stock cards and locks the store.

manas.q: Who is the first line in the three lines model?

children.note: Specialist teams that support and challenge the first line, e.g. a risk manager, a quality officer, a compliance team.
Gives independent assurance to the board on how well the first and second lines are working.

manas.q: What role does internal audit play in the three lines model?

children.note: Outside providers, such as external auditors and regulators, add another independent view from outside the organisation.
Internal audit cannot check everything, so it starts with the biggest risks. Then each assignment follows four steps.
Plan audit work around what could most hurt the organisation, not around a fixed rota.

manas.q: What is risk-based internal audit?

children.note: A simple way to rank risks: how likely is it, and how bad would it be? Score each 1–5 and multiply.

manas.q: What is a simple way to score a risk?

children.note: Management's list of key risks, owners and controls. Internal audit uses it to choose where to look.
A list of audits for the year, highest risks first, approved by the audit committee.
Agree the scope and objectives with the manager, learn how the process works and list the key risks and controls to test.

manas.q: What are the four steps of an internal audit assignment?

children.note: A short note saying what will be audited, the period covered, the team and the timetable.
Collect evidence: interview staff, walk through the process, inspect documents, count cash or stock and test samples.
Follow one transaction from start to finish, e.g. one loan from application to payout, to see how it really works.
Pick some items (e.g. 40 loan files) and check each control was done. Details are in the CPA auditing paper.
Record what was tested, what was found and who did it, so another auditor could reach the same result.
Write down findings, risks and recommendations, discuss them with management and get their agreed actions with dates.
A good finding states the Condition (what is), Criteria (what should be), Cause (why) and Consequence (so what).

manas.q: What are the parts of a good audit finding?

children.note: Most teams rate each finding high, medium or low so the board sees what matters most.
Later, check whether management really did what it promised. Unfixed high-risk issues go back to the audit committee.

manas.q: What happens at the follow-up stage of an internal audit?

children.note: Controls are the everyday checks that stop mistakes and theft. Internal audit tests whether they exist and work.
Any step that reduces a risk: a signature, a lock, a password, a count, a review.

manas.q: What is an internal control?

children.note: Preventive controls stop a problem (a locked store). Detective controls find it after (a monthly stock count).

manas.q: What is the difference between a preventive and a detective control?

children.note: Split a task so no one person controls it from start to end. The person who pays should not also record and approve.

manas.q: What is segregation of duties?

children.note: Important actions need approval by a named person with the right limit, e.g. loans above KES 500,000 need the credit committee.
Locks, safes, CCTV and restricted access to stores or cash.
Compare two records that should agree, e.g. the cash book with the bank statement, and investigate differences.
Three everyday places where controls matter.
Stock cards are updated on every issue; a person outside the pharmacy joins a surprise count; differences are explained and approved.
A fixed float (imprest), vouchers signed by the receiver and approved, surprise counts by someone other than the cashier.
Every file should hold the signed form, guarantor forms, payslip or income proof and credit committee approval before money is paid.
How internal audit works in Kenyan public bodies, and how to build a career in it.
This Kenyan law sets rules for managing public money. Under it, each public entity is expected to have an internal audit function.

manas.q: Which Kenyan law requires public entities to have internal audit?

children.note: Public bodies also have audit committees that receive internal audit reports and track whether issues are fixed.
Internal auditors work inside each body all year. The Office of the Auditor-General is the external auditor of public bodies.
The Institute of Internal Auditors is the worldwide professional body for internal auditors. It sets standards and offers certifications.

manas.q: What is the IIA?

children.note: Certified Internal Auditor (CIA) is the IIA's main professional certification.
Typical ladder: audit assistant → auditor → senior → audit manager → head of internal audit (chief audit executive). Many move into risk, finance or management.
Curiosity, clear writing, good questioning, basic IT and data skills, and the courage to report bad news politely.
Three small cases with KES figures that add up.
The auditor counts petty cash without warning, at a clinic with a KES 20,000 imprest.
Imprest float KES 20,000. Approved vouchers since the last top-up: KES 12,350. So cash in the box should be 20,000 − 12,350 = KES 7,650.
Notes and coins found: 5 × 1,000 = 5,000; 2 × 500 = 1,000; 1 × 100 = 100; coins 50. Total KES 6,150.
Expected 7,650 − counted 6,150 = KES 1,500 short. The cashier cannot explain it.
Until explained: Dr Staff receivable (cashier) KES 1,500 / Cr Petty cash KES 1,500. If written off later, Dr Cash shortage expense / Cr Staff receivable.
Cause: no surprise counts for 6 months. Recommend weekly surprise counts by the accountant and a signed count sheet.
A hospital pharmacy holds paracetamol boxes costed at KES 250 each.
Stock system shows 400 boxes = KES 100,000. Physical count finds 376 boxes = KES 94,000.
400 − 376 = 24 boxes missing; 24 × 250 = KES 6,000. Management must explain it before writing it off.
Issues to wards were not signed for. Recommend signed issue notes and monthly counts with someone from outside the pharmacy.
The auditor tests a sample of 40 loan files for complete guarantor forms.
6 of 40 files had no guarantor forms: 6 ÷ 40 = 15% of the sample failed the control.
The 6 loans: three of KES 150,000, two of KES 400,000 and one of KES 550,000 = KES 1,800,000 with no guarantors.
No payout until a checklist is signed by a second officer confirming all documents are on file.
Common mix-ups, then a few short questions to test yourself.

children.topic: Trap: internal audit is not external audit
children.note: Internal audit does not sign the opinion on the financial statements. That is the external auditor's job.
Internal audit recommends; management decides and acts. Doing the fix would harm independence.
Reporting only to the finance director weakens independence. The key line is to the audit committee.
A report with no follow-up often changes nothing. Follow-up is a real step of the job.
Give three differences between internal and external audit.
1) Who they serve: board/management vs shareholders. 2) Output: many reports vs one opinion. 3) Timing: all year vs mainly yearly; legal need differs too.
One clerk at a duka orders, receives and pays for stock. What control is missing?
Segregation of duties. Split ordering, receiving and paying between different people, or have the owner approve each payment.
Imprest KES 10,000; vouchers KES 6,800; cash counted KES 2,900. Find the shortfall.
Expected cash = 10,000 − 6,800 = KES 3,200. Shortfall = 3,200 − 2,900 = KES 300. Report it and ask the cashier to explain.

nodeData.note: Forensic accounting is accounting used to find, prove and explain fraud and money disputes. This map covers why people cheat, the common tricks, the warning signs, how an investigation runs and how a business protects itself.

children.topic: What it is and why it matters
children.note: Forensic accountants are money detectives. They check records closely enough that the findings can stand up in a dispute or in court.
It joins accounting skill with investigation skill: reading records, asking questions and proving what really happened to the money.

manas.q: What is forensic accounting?

children.note: Fraud is deliberately tricking someone to get money or an advantage. The word that matters is deliberately: an honest error is not fraud.

manas.q: What makes something fraud rather than an error?

children.note: A normal audit gives an opinion that the accounts are fair overall. Forensic work digs into a specific suspicion and follows it right to the end.

manas.q: How does a forensic investigation differ from a normal audit?

children.note: Fraud cases, insurance claims, business partner fights, divorce money disputes, valuing a lost business and checking claims against government.
Fraud quietly drains money from businesses, SACCOs, hospitals and government. Catching it early protects jobs, members' savings and public services.
The fraud triangle says three things usually come together before someone commits fraud: pressure, opportunity and an excuse.
Three sides: pressure (a need), opportunity (a way to do it) and rationalisation (an excuse that makes it feel OK). Remove one side and fraud is less likely.

manas.q: What are the three sides of the fraud triangle?

children.note: Debts, school fees, a gambling habit, a sick relative, or a boss demanding targets. The pressure is often hidden from colleagues.
One person handles cash and also records it, no one checks the payroll, or passwords are shared. Opportunity is the side a business controls best.

manas.q: Which side of the fraud triangle can a business control most easily?

children.note: 'I will pay it back', 'They underpay me anyway', 'Everyone does it'. The excuse lets an honest-seeming person cross the line.
A short, clear explanation of the three sides with simple examples.
Most frauds fall into three families: stealing assets, cooking the books, and corruption.
Employees taking cash, stock or other things the business owns. This is the most common kind of fraud, though each case is often small.

manas.q: What is asset misappropriation?

children.note: Taking cash before the sale is ever entered in the books, for example pocketing a duka sale and not ringing it up. There is no record to trace, so it is hard to spot.

manas.q: What is skimming?

children.note: A fake or departed worker kept on the payroll, with the pay going to the fraudster's bank account or M-Pesa number.

manas.q: What is a ghost employee?

children.note: A made-up supplier sends invoices for goods or services never delivered. The fraudster controls the supplier's bank account.

manas.q: What is a fake (shell) supplier fraud?

children.note: Financial statement fraud: making the accounts look better or worse than the truth, such as recording sales that never happened or hiding debts.

manas.q: What is financial statement fraud?

children.note: Bribes, kickbacks and conflicts of interest, such as a buyer giving a tender to a friend's company in return for a cut.

manas.q: What is a kickback?

children.note: Examples: a cashier pointing customers to a personal till number, fake 'reversal' requests, or paying a ghost worker's salary to a relative's phone number.
Warning signs in people and records, plus simple computer tests. A sign or test result is never proof on its own; it tells you where to look.
A warning sign that something might be wrong. On its own it proves nothing, but several together call for a closer look.

manas.q: What is a red flag in fraud work?

children.note: Living beyond their pay, never taking leave, refusing to share duties, being defensive when asked questions, or being very close to one supplier.
Missing documents, photocopies instead of originals, round-number payments, many corrections, entries late at night or at weekends.
Two staff sharing one bank account or phone number, workers with no leave or tax records, or staff no supervisor knows.
A supplier with only a P.O. box, no phone line, an address matching a staff member's, or invoices just under the approval limit.
In many real lists of numbers, more amounts start with 1 than with 9. Made-up numbers often break this pattern, which can flag a closer look.

manas.q: What does Benford's law say about first digits?

children.note: About 30% of amounts start with 1, about 18% with 2, and under 5% with 9. If every digit appears equally (about 11% each), that may be a sign of invented figures.
Sort payments by supplier, amount and invoice number. The same invoice paid twice can be an error or a fraud.

manas.q: What is a duplicate payment test?

children.note: Look for many exact round sums, or many payments just under an approval limit, such as KES 49,900 when the limit is KES 50,000.
Compare the payroll with the staff list, and supplier bank details with staff bank details. A match where none should exist is a red flag.
Entries posted on Sundays, public holidays or at 2 am deserve a look, since normal work rarely happens then.
An investigation moves step by step: plan, collect evidence, follow the money, interview people, then write a report.
Decide what is suspected, who knows and what to look at. Keep it confidential so evidence is not destroyed and innocent people are not harmed.
Collect documents, bank and M-Pesa statements, emails and computer records, and keep them safe so they are not changed.

manas.q: What does 'gathering evidence' cover in a fraud investigation?

children.note: A record of who held each piece of evidence and when. It shows a court the evidence was not tampered with.

manas.q: What is the chain of custody?

children.note: Following each shilling from where it left the business to where it ended up, through bank accounts, M-Pesa numbers and purchases.

manas.q: What does 'tracing the money' mean?

children.note: Talk to neutral witnesses first and the suspect last, once the facts are known. Stay calm, ask open questions and write everything down.
A clear written report of the findings and the loss, which a forensic accountant may have to explain in court. It must be fair, not take sides.

manas.q: What is an expert witness report?

children.note: The accountant reports what the evidence shows. Deciding guilt is for the court, not the accountant.
Invented examples with KES figures that add up. Check each line yourself.
A clinic has 40 real staff costing KES 1,300,000 a month. From March a clerk adds a fake worker 'K. Otieno' paid KES 32,500 a month to a phone number the clerk controls.
Payroll recorded each month = 1,300,000 real + 32,500 ghost = KES 1,332,500. The extra is small enough not to stand out.
Found at the end of October. March to October is 8 months: 8 × 32,500 = KES 260,000 lost. Over a full year it would have been 12 × 32,500 = KES 390,000.

children.topic: Ghost worker: how it was traced
children.note: A matching test showed the 'worker' and the clerk shared one M-Pesa number, and no supervisor or leave record existed for the worker.
If recovery from the clerk is expected: Dr Amount due from employee KES 260,000 / Cr Salaries expense KES 260,000. If not recoverable, it stays as a loss.
Stock costing KES 900,000 was sold at cost + 25%, so sales should be 900,000 × 1.25 = KES 1,125,000. Only KES 1,050,000 was recorded: a gap of KES 75,000 to explain.
Supplier invoice no. 2231 for KES 48,600 was paid twice. Total paid 2 × 48,600 = KES 97,200, so KES 48,600 must be recovered from the supplier.
Benford expects about 30.1% to start with 1, so about 301 payments. Finding only 120 is far off the pattern and worth a closer look, not proof.
Prevention is cheaper than investigation. Good controls take away the 'opportunity' side of the triangle.
Segregation of duties: the person who handles cash should not also record it or approve payments. Then one person cannot cheat alone.

manas.q: What is segregation of duties?

children.note: Payments above a set amount need a second person to approve. Check that limits are not dodged by splitting invoices.
Match bank and M-Pesa statements to the books every month, and count cash and stock by surprise.
Check new staff and new suppliers before they are added, and review the lists regularly for people who left or suppliers no one uses.
A safe, private way for staff to report worries without fear of punishment. Tips are one of the main ways fraud is found.

manas.q: Why is whistle-blowing important?

children.note: When leaders act honestly and punish cheating fairly, staff follow. A code of conduct and training support this.
Make staff take their leave and let someone else do the job meanwhile. Many frauds come out when the fraudster is away.
How fraud is handled in Kenya in general terms, the CFE qualification and where forensic accountants work.
The Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission fights and prevents corruption, especially in public bodies, through investigation and education.

manas.q: What does the EACC do?

children.note: The Directorate of Criminal Investigations is the police arm that investigates crimes, including fraud, in Kenya.
The Proceeds of Crime and Anti-Money Laundering Act deals with hiding the source of criminal money and with taking such money back.
Making stolen money look clean by passing it through accounts, businesses or property so its source is hidden.

manas.q: What is money laundering?

children.note: M-Pesa records show who sent what, to whom and when. They are often key evidence for tracing money in Kenya.

nodeData.note: How governments, counties and public bodies keep and report the accounts for public money. The aim is not profit but showing citizens that money was raised and spent as the law and the budget allowed.

children.topic: What it is and why it matters
children.note: Public sector accounting records the money of governments and the bodies they own. It answers one big question: did they use our money as promised?
Accounting for national and county governments, ministries, state corporations and other public bodies. It records taxes and grants received and money spent on public services.

manas.q: What is public sector accounting?

children.topic: Who is in the public sector
children.note: Ministries and departments, county governments, state corporations (like public hospitals, universities and water companies), and independent offices and commissions.

manas.q: Name four kinds of public sector bodies in Kenya.

children.note: A business tries to make a profit for its owners. A government tries to deliver services such as roads, clinics and schools with the money it has.

manas.q: How does the aim of a public body differ from a business?

children.note: The 'owners' are the citizens and taxpayers. Accounts are published so that Parliament, the public and the media can check how money was used.
Once Parliament or a county assembly passes the budget, it becomes a legal limit. Spending more, or on something else, without approval breaks the law, not just a plan.

manas.q: Why is a government budget different from a business budget?

children.note: Mostly taxes, fees and charges, borrowing, and grants from donors. Counties also get a share of national revenue sent from the national government.
Business: profit, shareholders, IFRS, budget is a guide. Public body: service, citizens, IPSAS, budget is a legal limit.
There are two main ways to decide when to record income and spending. Governments are slowly moving from cash to accrual.
Records income only when cash comes in and spending only when cash goes out. Simple, but it hides unpaid bills and the cost of using up assets.

manas.q: What is the cash basis of accounting?

children.note: Records income when earned and costs when incurred, whether or not cash has moved. It shows debts owed, assets owned and their wear and tear.

manas.q: What is the accrual basis of accounting?

children.note: A county can look as if it has money left over while it owes suppliers a lot. Those unpaid bills (pending bills) do not show in cash accounts.

manas.q: What are pending bills?

children.note: Accrual gives a fuller picture: what the government owns, what it owes and the full cost of each service. This helps better decisions and fewer surprises.
Some governments use a halfway house: mostly cash, with a few items such as payables added, or mostly accrual with some items left out.

children.topic: The rules: IPSAS and Kenya's PSASB
children.note: Public bodies follow their own set of accounting standards, adapted from business standards to fit government.
International Public Sector Accounting Standards: a global set of accounting rules for public bodies. They are based on IFRS but adjusted for things like taxes and grants.

manas.q: What does IPSAS stand for?

children.note: The International Public Sector Accounting Standards Board (IPSASB) writes IPSAS. It works with support from IFAC, the global body of accountants.

manas.q: Which board issues IPSAS?

children.topic: Accrual IPSAS and Cash Basis IPSAS
children.note: There is a full set of accrual IPSAS, plus a separate Cash Basis IPSAS for governments not yet ready for accrual.
Kenya's Public Sector Accounting Standards Board (PSASB) sets the accounting and reporting framework for Kenyan public entities. It issues the standards and reporting templates they must use.

manas.q: What does Kenya's PSASB do?

children.note: The main Kenyan law on how public money is planned, spent, accounted for and reported. It also set up the PSASB.
Many ministries and counties have reported on a cash-based IPSAS framework, while many state corporations use accrual IPSAS. Check PSASB's current guidance, as a move to accrual is under way.
Exchange income is a fair swap, like a hospital fee. Non-exchange income comes with nothing directly given back, like taxes and grants. IPSAS treats them differently.

manas.q: What is non-exchange revenue?

children.note: Public money moves in a yearly cycle: plan, approve, spend, account, audit. Kenya's financial year runs from 1 July to 30 June.
Kenya has a national government and 47 county governments. Each prepares, passes and spends its own budget.

manas.q: What are Kenya's two levels of government?

children.note: The National Treasury, and each county treasury, asks departments for their needs and puts together the budget proposals and strategy papers.
Parliament approves the national budget and each county assembly approves its county budget. The approved budget becomes law (an appropriation law).

manas.q: Who approves the national and county budgets in Kenya?

children.note: Before money leaves the main government funds, the Controller of Budget checks the withdrawal is allowed by law and approves it. Departments then spend.

manas.q: What is the role of the Controller of Budget?

children.note: Accounting officers keep records and prepare financial statements. The Controller of Budget also publishes regular reports on how budgets are being used.
The Auditor-General, through the Office of the Auditor-General, audits public bodies and reports whether the accounts are fair and money was used lawfully.

manas.q: What does the Auditor-General do?

children.note: Parliament and county assemblies, through their accounts committees, study the audit reports, question officers and recommend action.
The National Treasury manages national public finances, prepares the budget and oversees the accounting rules and systems. Each county has its own county treasury.
Controller of Budget looks before and during spending (may this money go out?). Auditor-General looks after (was it used properly and recorded fairly?).

children.topic: Tools and ideas used in government
children.note: Some tools and ideas you will meet in public sector finance offices.
Integrated Financial Management Information System: Kenya's government-wide computer system for budgets, buying, payments and reports.

manas.q: What is IFMIS?

children.note: Money given for a set purpose is kept in its own fund, a self-balancing set of accounts, so it can be shown that it was used only for that purpose.

manas.q: What is fund accounting?

children.note: The budget is split into votes and lines (for example, 'roads maintenance'). Spending is charged to the correct line and checked against its limit.
Moving approved money from one budget line to another. It is only allowed within set limits and with the right approval.

manas.q: What is a virement?

children.note: Actual spending divided by the budget, as a percentage. A low rate may mean projects stalled; above 100% means overspending.

manas.q: How is the absorption rate calculated?

children.note: A key report that sets the approved budget beside what was really received and spent, showing the differences (variances).
Two short examples with KES figures that add up.

children.topic: Example 1: a ward's budget vs actual
children.note: A county ward's development budget for one year was KES 9,500,000. Actual spending was KES 9,300,000.
Roads grading: budget 4,000,000, actual 3,600,000. Water point: 2,500,000 vs 2,750,000. Dispensary drugs: 1,200,000 vs 1,150,000. Bursaries: 1,800,000 vs 1,800,000.
Roads: 400,000 under. Water point: 250,000 over (10% overspend). Drugs: 50,000 under. Bursaries: nil.
Why did roads underspend: was work skipped? Was the 250,000 water overspend approved by a virement? An auditor would ask both.

children.topic: Example 2: cash vs accrual, same year
children.note: A county health department's year: grant received KES 50,000,000; salaries paid 30,000,000; suppliers paid 12,000,000.
Cash in 50,000,000 − salaries 30,000,000 − suppliers 12,000,000 = cash surplus 8,000,000.
Drugs worth 3,000,000 were received but not paid by year end. Dr Medical supplies expense 3,000,000 / Cr Payables 3,000,000.
Of the 12,000,000 paid to suppliers, 500,000 is rent for next year. Dr Prepayments 500,000 / Cr Rent expense 500,000.
An ambulance bought in an earlier year wears out by 1,500,000 this year. Dr Depreciation expense 1,500,000 / Cr Accumulated depreciation 1,500,000.
8,000,000 − 3,000,000 + 500,000 − 1,500,000 = 4,000,000. Accrual shows half the 'surplus' of cash, because of the unpaid bill and wear and tear.
A county bursary fund receives 2,000,000 and pays 1,800,000 to students. The 200,000 left stays in the fund for bursaries only; it cannot be used to pay for roads.
After an audit, the Auditor-General gives an opinion on the accounts. Kenyan audit reports on ministries and counties use these same types.
The accounts are fair in all important ways. This is the best result.

manas.q: What is an unmodified audit opinion?

children.note: The accounts are fair except for one or more specific problems, for example spending without proper documents.

manas.q: What is a qualified audit opinion?

children.note: The problems are so big and widespread that the accounts as a whole are not fair.

manas.q: What is an adverse audit opinion?

children.note: The auditor could not get enough evidence to give any opinion at all, often because records were missing.

manas.q: What is a disclaimer of opinion?

children.note: Public audit also checks whether spending was lawful and gave good value, not only whether the figures are right.
Mix-ups that cost marks and cause wrong judgements.
A surplus may just mean projects were not done. In public bodies, low spending can be a failure of service.
Cash accounts leave out unpaid bills and assets. Always ask about pending bills.
The Controller of Budget approves withdrawals and monitors budgets; the Auditor-General audits afterwards. Do not swap them.
Charging costs to a line with spare money, without a virement, breaks budget rules even if the total is within budget.
A qualified opinion is not clean. Only an unmodified opinion is.
Public bodies talk of surplus or deficit, not profit, and follow IPSAS, not IFRS.
Try each one before opening the answer steps.
Budget KES 2,500,000; actual KES 2,750,000. Find the variance and say if it is over or under.
Actual is more than budget, so it is a 250,000 overspend, which is 250,000 ÷ 2,500,000 = 10%.
It needs approval (for example a virement or supplementary budget); otherwise it is unauthorised spending.
Cash surplus KES 6,000,000. Unpaid bills at year end 1,200,000; depreciation 800,000. Find the accrual surplus.
List the four types of audit opinion and one-line meaning of each.
Unmodified: fair. Qualified: fair except for some items. Adverse: not fair. Disclaimer: no opinion possible.

nodeData.note: How businesses count their effect on nature: environmental costs, greenhouse gas emissions (scopes 1, 2, 3) and carbon credits, with simple worked examples and Kenyan context.

children.topic: What it is and why it matters
children.note: Environmental and carbon accounting tracks how a business affects nature, in money and in physical units like tonnes of gas.
Measuring and reporting the money and non-money effects of a business on the environment, such as waste, water and pollution.

manas.q: What is environmental accounting?

children.note: Measuring and tracking how much greenhouse gas an organisation puts into the air, so it can set targets and cut it.

manas.q: What is carbon accounting?

children.note: One view shows nature's effect on the business in shillings. The other shows the business's effect on nature in kg, litres or tonnes.

manas.q: What are the two sides of an environmental accounting system?

children.note: Investors, banks, big customers, regulators and the public want to know climate risks and how a firm is cutting its emissions.
Accountants already collect data on fuel, power and travel bills. That same data drives the carbon numbers, so the skills fit well.
Kenya faces droughts and floods linked to climate change, so lenders and buyers increasingly ask Kenyan firms for climate data.
Costs a business pays because of its effect on the environment. Many are hidden inside general overheads.

children.topic: What counts as an environmental cost
children.note: Waste handling, clean-up of polluted land, environmental fines and taxes, pollution-control equipment and site restoration.

manas.q: Give four examples of environmental costs.

children.note: Environmental costs are often buried in general overheads, so managers do not see them or try to reduce them.
Prevention costs stop pollution before it happens (filters, training). Failure costs come after (clean-up, fines). Prevention is usually cheaper.

manas.q: What is the difference between environmental prevention and failure costs?

children.note: Using cost tools inside the firm to find, track and cut environmental costs. It appears in management accounting papers.

manas.q: What is environmental management accounting (EMA)?

children.note: If a firm must restore a site later, it records a provision (IAS 37) and adds the cost to the asset (IAS 16).
Activity-based costing, flow cost accounting (tracking materials and waste) and life-cycle costing help find environmental costs.
The GHG Protocol sorts a company's emissions into three groups called scopes, so everyone counts the same way.
Gases that trap heat in the air, such as carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide. They are all converted to one unit: CO2e.
One common unit that adds all greenhouse gases together by how strongly each warms the planet compared with CO2.

manas.q: What does CO2e mean?

children.note: The main global standard for counting company emissions. WRI and WBCSD published its first version in 2001.

manas.q: Who created the GHG Protocol and when?

children.note: Emissions from sources the business owns or controls, like its own generator, boiler or delivery vans burning fuel.

manas.q: What are Scope 1 emissions?

children.note: Emissions caused by producing the electricity, heat or steam the business buys, e.g. its Kenya Power bill.

manas.q: What are Scope 2 emissions?

children.note: All other indirect emissions: suppliers, transport by others, staff commuting, business flights, waste, and customers using products.

manas.q: What are Scope 3 emissions?

children.note: For most firms Scope 3 is the largest and hardest to measure, because the data sits with suppliers and customers.
Scope 1 = I burn it. Scope 2 = I buy the power. Scope 3 = everyone else in my chain burns it.

manas.q: Give a simple trick to remember scopes 1, 2 and 3.

children.note: ISO 14064 is another standard for measuring and checking emissions. It uses similar groups to the GHG Protocol.
A carbon footprint is the total greenhouse gas a person, product or company adds to the air, shown in CO2e.
Emissions = activity data × emission factor. Example: litres of diesel × kg CO2e per litre.

manas.q: What is the basic formula for calculating emissions?

children.note: The amount of something used: litres of fuel, kWh of power, km travelled, kg of waste. Often taken from bills and invoices.

manas.q: What is activity data?

children.note: A number saying how much CO2e comes from one unit of activity, e.g. kg CO2e per litre. Use official published factors.

manas.q: What is an emission factor?

children.note: Divide kg by 1,000 to get tonnes. 2,500 kg CO2e = 2.5 tonnes CO2e (tCO2e).

manas.q: How do you convert kg CO2e to tonnes?

children.note: 1) Set the boundary. 2) List sources by scope. 3) Collect activity data. 4) Multiply by factors. 5) Add up and report.
Pick a base year to compare against, then set a target such as cutting emissions 20% from that year.

manas.q: Why do companies set a base year?

children.note: Emissions divided by a measure of size, like revenue or units made. It lets you compare firms of different sizes.

manas.q: What is emissions intensity?

children.note: Practice with simple numbers. All emission factors here are made up for learning only. Use official factors in real work.
A duka's generator burns 200 litres of diesel. Factor 2.7 kg CO2e per litre (illustrative made-up factor, not an official figure). 200 × 2.7 = 540 kg = 0.54 tCO2e.
An office uses 10,000 kWh in a year. Factor 0.1 kg CO2e per kWh (illustrative made-up factor, not an official figure). 10,000 × 0.1 = 1,000 kg = 1.0 tCO2e.
Three owned matatus use 12,000 litres of diesel a year. Factor 2.7 kg per litre (illustrative made-up factor, not an official figure). 12,000 × 2.7 = 32,400 kg = 32.4 tCO2e.
Staff travel 5,000 km by car to work. Factor 0.2 kg CO2e per km (illustrative made-up factor, not an official figure). 5,000 × 0.2 = 1,000 kg = 1.0 tCO2e.
Generator 0.54 t (Scope 1) + power 1.0 t (Scope 2) + commuting 1.0 t (Scope 3) = 2.54 tCO2e in total.
0.54 + 1.00 = 1.54; 1.54 + 1.00 = 2.54 tCO2e. Always show each scope separately, then the total.
Revenue KES 10 million. 2.54 t ÷ 10 = 0.254 tCO2e per KES 1 million of revenue.
If the office in example 2 gets half its power from its own solar, Scope 2 falls to 5,000 × 0.1 = 500 kg = 0.5 t.
A factory pays KES 30,000 to a licensed waste handler. Dr Waste disposal expense 30,000 / Cr Bank 30,000.
A quarry must restore land later; present value KES 500,000. Dr Quarry asset 500,000 / Cr Provision for restoration 500,000.
A firm buys 10 credits at KES 2,000 each. Dr Carbon credits (asset) 20,000 / Cr Bank 20,000. Expense them when retired.
Ways to put a price on carbon so cutting emissions pays off.
A tradable certificate showing 1 tonne of CO2e was avoided or removed from the air, e.g. by a forest or clean-cookstove project.

manas.q: One carbon credit represents what?

children.note: Buying credits to balance out your own emissions. It does not cut your actual emissions, so report gross emissions too.

manas.q: What is carbon offsetting?

children.note: Using a credit up so it cannot be sold again. The buyer then claims the tonne against its emissions.
Voluntary: firms buy credits by choice. Compliance: the law caps emissions, e.g. the EU Emissions Trading Scheme.

manas.q: What is the difference between voluntary and compliance carbon markets?

children.note: Government sets a limit and gives out allowances. Firms below the limit can sell spare allowances to firms above it.
Some credits are weak: the cut would have happened anyway (no additionality), or two parties claim the same tonne.
There is no specific IFRS for carbon credits yet, so firms pick a policy, often an intangible or inventory, and disclose it.
In 2024 Kenya brought in carbon market regulations under the Climate Change Act, with a National Carbon Registry for credits.

children.topic: Reporting: IFRS S1, S2 and Kenya
children.note: How carbon numbers reach investors and regulators.
ISSB standard asking firms to disclose sustainability risks and opportunities that could affect their cash flows and value.

manas.q: What does IFRS S1 cover?

children.note: ISSB standard on climate risks. It asks for Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions, targets and climate strategy. See the Sustainability reporting map.

manas.q: Which emissions does IFRS S2 ask for?

children.note: Auditors can give assurance on emissions data, like an audit of accounts, to make it more reliable.
Kenya's main climate law. It set up a National Climate Change Council, chaired by the President, to guide low-carbon development.
The NSE joined the UN Sustainable Stock Exchanges initiative in 2015 and promotes ESG and green finance for listed firms.
Kenya plans mandatory IFRS sustainability reporting, with IFRS S2 expected around 2027. Check ICPAK for the latest timeline.
Errors students and preparers make most often.
Burning your own fuel is Scope 1. Buying electricity is Scope 2, even though the power station burns the fuel.
Factors are often in kg. Divide by 1,000 before reporting in tonnes, or you overstate by 1,000 times.
Do not report only net emissions. Show gross emissions, then credits used, then the net figure.
Many firms skip Scope 3 because it is hard. Exams expect you to name it and explain why it matters.
Factors differ by country and year. Kenya's grid is mostly renewable, so a foreign grid factor would be wrong.
Environmental fines are failure costs. Separate them so managers see the cost of poor control.
Try each question, then open the answer steps.
Classify: own delivery van, purchased electricity, supplier transport, staff business flights, own boiler.
Scope 1: own van, own boiler. Scope 2: purchased electricity. Scope 3: supplier transport, business flights.
Diesel 1,000 litres at 2.7 kg/l; power 20,000 kWh at 0.1 kg/kWh (illustrative made-up factor, not an official figure). Find total tCO2e.
A firm emits 4.7 t and buys and retires 3 credits. What does it report?
Gross 4.7 tCO2e; credits retired 3 t; net 4.7 − 3 = 1.7 tCO2e. Gross must still be shown.
Why should a manager separate environmental costs from overheads?
So the costs are visible, charged to the products that cause them, and can be cut. Hidden costs distort prices.
