nodeData.note: Social and impact accounting measures and reports the good and harm an organisation does to people and the planet, not just its profit. You will learn the results chain, SROI with a KES example, the triple bottom line, GRI and impact investing.

children.topic: What it is and why it matters
children.note: Social accounting tells the story of how an organisation affects people and nature, not just how much profit it made.
Measuring and reporting the effects an organisation has on people, communities and the environment, beyond money in the bank. It is also called non-financial reporting or CSR reporting.

manas.q: What is social accounting?

children.note: A profit and loss account shows sales and costs. It does not show that a clinic saved lives or that a factory polluted a river.
The SACCO's accounts show fares and fuel. They do not show that members' children now go to school because drivers earn steady pay.
Companies (for CSR), NGOs and charities, SACCOs and co-operatives, government agencies and donors all use social accounting.
Donors and investors want proof that money did good. It also helps managers see what works, so they can do more of it and stop what fails.
In the 20th century 'social accounting' also meant counting a country's national income and wealth. Today it usually means social and environmental reporting.

manas.q: What did 'social accounting' mean in the older, 20th-century sense?

children.note: Social accounting starts by asking who is touched by the work and listening to them.
Any person or group affected by, or able to affect, an organisation: members, staff, customers, the community, donors, government.

manas.q: What is a stakeholder?

children.note: Good social accounting talks to the people affected. A youth project should ask the youth what changed for them.
Members (savers and borrowers), staff, the board, the regulator, the local community and lenders to the SACCO.
Beneficiaries (the people helped), donors, volunteers, county government and partner groups.
Stakeholders may be harmed as well as helped, e.g. a new road cuts travel time but displaces some kiosks. Both sides belong in the account.
To measure change you need clear steps: what you put in, what you did, and what changed because of it.
Inputs → activities → outputs → outcomes → impact. Each step leads to the next.

manas.q: Name the five steps of the results chain.

children.note: What you put in: money, staff, time, equipment. Example: KES 1,000,000 and two trainers.

manas.q: What are inputs?

children.note: What you do with the inputs. Example: running tailoring classes for youth.
The direct, countable products of the work. Example: 30 youth trained, 300 class hours held.

manas.q: What is an output?

children.note: The changes in people's lives that follow. Example: 20 youth got jobs and earn more.

manas.q: What is an outcome?

children.note: The part of the change that happened only because of you, often long-term. Example: lower youth poverty in the ward, after removing what would have happened anyway.

manas.q: What is impact (in impact measurement)?

children.note: 'We gave out 1,000 mosquito nets' is an output. 'Malaria cases fell' is an outcome. Funders now want outcomes.
A simple map showing how and why your activities are expected to lead to the change you want. It spells out each step and the assumptions behind it.

manas.q: What is a theory of change?

children.note: Give pads (activity) → girls miss fewer school days (outcome) → better grades and later marriage (impact). Assumption: missing pads was the real reason for absence.
If girls miss school mainly because of fees, pads alone will not work. A theory of change makes such weak links visible.
A measurable sign of change, such as 'number of members with savings above KES 10,000' or 'school attendance rate'.

manas.q: What is an indicator?

children.note: The situation before the project starts. Without a baseline you cannot show what changed.

manas.q: What is a baseline?

children.note: SROI puts a shilling value on social change and compares it with what was spent.
A method that gives money values (proxies) to social and environmental changes and compares the total with the money invested. Social Value UK promotes the standard method.

manas.q: What is Social Return on Investment (SROI)?

children.note: SROI ratio = present value of social benefits ÷ value of the investment. A ratio of 3:1 means KES 3 of social value for every KES 1 spent.

manas.q: What is the SROI ratio formula?

children.note: A money value used for something with no market price, e.g. using the cost of a clinic visit avoided to value better health.

manas.q: What is a financial proxy in SROI?

children.note: The share of the change that would have happened anyway without the project. You subtract it.

manas.q: What is deadweight in SROI?

children.note: The share of the change caused by others (government, other NGOs, family). You subtract it too.

manas.q: What is attribution in SROI?

children.note: How much the benefit fades each year after the first. Example: 20% drop-off means each year is worth 80% of the year before.

manas.q: What is drop-off in SROI?

children.note: When your good result just moves a problem elsewhere, e.g. your trainees take jobs others would have had. Some of the value is removed.
Future shillings are worth less than today's, so later years' benefits are discounted to present value. Simple class examples often skip this.
Real numbers in KES. Check every line adds up.
An NGO spends KES 1,000,000 training 30 youth. 20 get jobs earning an extra KES 5,000 a month. Deadweight 25%, attribution 10%, benefit lasts 3 years, drop-off 20% a year, no discounting.
20 youth × KES 5,000 × 12 months = KES 1,200,000 extra income in year 1.
1,976,400 ÷ 1,000,000 = 1.98. About KES 1.98 of social value for each KES 1 spent (roughly 2:1).

A Nyeri dairy SACCO reports: 1,200 members, KES 45m in loans, 300 loans used for dairy cows, 85 members' children supported with school-fee loans. These are outputs; the next step is asking members what changed (outcomes).
A bank donates KES 200,000 to a children's ward. Dr Donations (CSR) expense 200,000 / Cr Bank 200,000. The money side balances; the social account then reports what the donation achieved.
Profit: KES 300,000 a year. People: employs 2 local staff, pays on time. Planet: switched to paper bags, saving 5,000 plastic bags a year. All three are reported together.
Bigger frameworks help organisations report social effects in a standard way.
Judge an organisation on three results: people (social), planet (environment) and profit (economic). John Elkington says he coined the phrase in 1994.

manas.q: What are the three parts of the triple bottom line?

children.note: Free global standards from the Global Reporting Initiative for reporting an organisation's impacts on economy, environment and people. Founded in 1997, first guidelines in 2000.

manas.q: What are the GRI Standards?

children.topic: How GRI works in plain terms
children.note: Universal standards apply to everyone; sector standards cover industries; topic standards cover items like labour, water or anti-corruption. You report the topics that matter most (material topics).
Thousands of organisations in over 100 countries, including most of the world's largest companies. Some Kenyan firms use it too.
Report what matters most: the impacts that are largest for people and nature, or most important to stakeholders.

manas.q: What does materiality mean in impact reporting?

children.note: Investing in businesses, funds or NGOs with the aim of a measurable social or environmental good as well as a financial return.

manas.q: What is impact investing?

children.note: Investors back off-grid solar firms, affordable clinics and microfinance lenders in Kenya, expecting both a return and proof of benefit, e.g. homes lit or patients served.
ESG screening mainly asks how social and green risks affect the investor. Impact investing aims to cause a positive change and measure it.
Corporate social responsibility: companies' voluntary work for society, e.g. bursaries, water projects, tree planting and health camps run through company foundations.
Where social accounts go wrong, and where exam answers lose marks.
Claiming more social good than you actually create, to win funds or look good. It is the social cousin of greenwashing.

manas.q: What is impact-washing?

children.note: Marketing that misleads people into thinking a product or firm is greener than it is.

manas.q: What is greenwashing?

children.note: Saying '500 people trained' proves impact. It does not; you must show what changed and why.
Claiming all change as yours. Some would have happened anyway, so the SROI ratio gets inflated.
Reporting only good stories and hiding harm or failures. Good social accounts show both.

children.topic: Ratio is not the whole story
children.note: A 5:1 SROI from weak proxies is less reliable than a 2:1 from careful data. Always state your assumptions.
Social reports without outside assurance are easier to inflate. Ask whether an independent party reviewed them.
Try each one, then open the answer steps.
A clinic runs 50 nutrition talks; child stunting in the area falls by 5%, of which half is due to a government programme. Classify each part.
50 talks = output. Stunting falls 5% = outcome. The 2.5% left after removing the government's share = impact.
A water project costs KES 500,000 and creates social value with present value KES 1,500,000. Find the SROI ratio.
SROI ratio = value ÷ investment = 1,500,000 ÷ 500,000 = 3.
State it as 3:1, KES 3 of social value for each KES 1 invested. Net value created = 1,500,000 − 500,000 = KES 1,000,000.
Gross benefit KES 800,000; deadweight 20%; attribution 25%. Find the impact.
Explain the triple bottom line to a SACCO board in three points.
People: member welfare and staff. Planet: environmental effects, e.g. green loans. Profit: surplus and financial strength. Report all three, not profit alone.

nodeData.note: How finance works under Islamic rules: no interest, real assets, shared risk. You learn the main contracts, how to record them in KES, zakat basics and the Kenyan scene.

children.topic: What it is and why it matters
children.note: Islamic finance is money and business done in a way that follows Sharia (Islamic law). It serves Muslim customers, but anyone can use it, and it is growing in Kenya.
Banking, saving, investing and insurance arranged so they fit Islamic rules on fairness and trade. It is also called Sharia-compliant finance.

manas.q: What is Islamic finance?

children.note: Muslim families and businesses who want to avoid interest, plus non-Muslims who like its asset-backed, share-the-risk style.
The deals look different from a normal loan, so the entries, the names of accounts and sometimes the standards differ. You must record the real substance correctly.
These are religious rules held sincerely by many people. Scholars differ on some details, so real products are approved by a Sharia board of qualified scholars.
A few big ideas shape every Islamic finance deal. Learn these first and the contracts make sense.
Riba means unfair gain from lending money, and most Muslims take it to include all interest on loans. So money must not earn money just by being lent.

manas.q: What is riba?

children.note: Gharar is too much uncertainty in a contract, like selling fish not yet caught. Price, item and terms must be clear to both sides.

manas.q: What is gharar?

children.note: Gain must not come from pure chance or betting. This is one reason normal insurance is replaced by takaful.

manas.q: What is maysir?

children.note: Money must not fund things Islam forbids, such as alcohol, pork or gambling. Banks screen customers and investments for this.
Profit is earned by taking part in real business risk, not by a fixed return no matter what. Partners share profit and bear losses fairly.

manas.q: Why is risk-sharing central in Islamic finance?

children.note: Most deals involve a real thing: goods bought and sold, a building rented, or a business owned together. Money is a tool, not something to trade for itself.
Islamic banks use a set of contract types. Each one replaces a conventional product with a sale, a lease or a partnership.
The bank buys an item, then sells it to you at cost plus an agreed profit, paid now or in instalments. The price is fixed at the start.

manas.q: What is murabaha?

children.note: The bank buys an asset and rents it to you for agreed rent. The bank owns it and carries ownership risk; some deals end with you owning it.

manas.q: What is ijara?

children.note: Two or more partners put in money and share profit by an agreed ratio. Losses are shared in line with how much capital each put in.

manas.q: What is musharaka?

children.note: One side gives the money (rabb-ul-mal), the other runs the business (mudarib). Profit is split by an agreed ratio; money losses fall on the investor unless the manager was careless.

manas.q: What is mudaraba?

children.note: Certificates that give holders a share in real assets or a project. Holders earn profit or rent from those assets instead of interest, so sukuk work like a Sharia-compliant bond.

manas.q: What are sukuk?

children.note: Members pay contributions into a shared fund that pays members who suffer a loss. An operator manages the fund. It replaces normal insurance.

manas.q: What is takaful?

children.note: A deposit held safely for the owner. Current accounts in Islamic banks are often run this way, with no interest paid.
The books show a sale, a lease or a partnership, not a loan with interest. Account names change, and profit is spread over time in a fair way.
Income is called murabaha profit, ijara rent or a share of business profit. You never book 'interest income' on Islamic products.

manas.q: What does an Islamic bank book instead of interest income?

children.note: In a murabaha on instalments, the agreed profit is first held back as deferred profit. It moves into income bit by bit as time passes.

manas.q: What is deferred murabaha profit?

children.note: Before a murabaha sale or during an ijara, the bank holds the item as its own asset. This must show on its balance sheet.

children.topic: No extra charge for late payment
children.note: The murabaha price cannot grow if the customer pays late. Many banks make late payers give a set amount to charity instead, so the bank earns nothing extra.
Some deposits share in the bank's profit and loss, like mudaraba. Reports show these separately from ordinary debts because the holders share risk.
A Sharia supervisory board checks products follow the rules. Reports often include its review alongside the normal audit report.
Two families of rules guide reporting. Which one applies depends on the country.
The Accounting and Auditing Organization for Islamic Financial Institutions, based in Bahrain. It issues Sharia, accounting, auditing and governance standards for Islamic finance.

manas.q: What is AAOIFI?

children.note: AAOIFI's Financial Accounting Standards cover topics like murabaha, ijara, sukuk, zakat and takaful. Some countries make them compulsory for Islamic banks.
International Financial Reporting Standards, issued by the IASB. Kenyan banks, including Islamic ones, generally report under IFRS.

manas.q: Which standards do Kenyan banks generally report under?

children.note: Under IFRS you look at the substance: a murabaha receivable is a financial asset (IFRS 9), and leases follow IFRS 16. AAOIFI adds detail on Sharia features that IFRS does not cover.
Whatever the framework, explain the contract types, Sharia board review, and how profit is shared and recognised. Users should see the deal's real nature.
Zakat is a yearly giving to the needy, one of the Five Pillars of Islam. Accountants are often asked to help work it out.
A required charitable payment for Muslims whose wealth is above a minimum level. It goes to set groups, such as the poor, the needy and people in debt.

manas.q: What is zakat?

children.note: Nisab is the wealth level below which no zakat is due. Scholars differ on how to set it, so check with a trusted scholar or body.

manas.q: What is nisab?

children.note: Zakat on wealth is customarily 2.5% (one fortieth) of qualifying wealth held for a year. Details differ between scholars.

manas.q: What is the customary zakat rate on wealth?

children.note: A business often adds cash, stock for sale and money owed to it, then takes away short-term debts. Zakat is worked out on what is left.
In Kenya zakat is a religious duty, not a KRA tax. Keep it separate from income tax in your workings.
Real numbers in KES. Check each entry: debits must equal credits.

children.topic: Murabaha: a pickup for a duka
children.note: Amina needs a pickup for her duka. The bank buys it from a dealer for KES 2,000,000 and sells it to her for KES 2,300,000, paid in 10 monthly instalments of KES 230,000.
Cost KES 2,000,000 + agreed profit KES 300,000 = sale price KES 2,300,000. Fixed at the start and cannot rise.
Dr Murabaha asset (pickup held) 2,000,000 / Cr Cash 2,000,000. The bank owns it for a short time.
Dr Murabaha receivable 2,300,000 / Cr Murabaha asset 2,000,000 / Cr Deferred murabaha profit 300,000. Debits 2,300,000 = credits 2,300,000.
Dr Cash 230,000 / Cr Murabaha receivable 230,000. After 10 months the receivable is zero.
Dr Deferred murabaha profit 30,000 / Cr Murabaha profit income 30,000 (300,000 ÷ 10). Real banks often spread it by the balance still owed, which earns more early on.
Dr Vehicle 2,000,000 / Dr Deferred murabaha cost 300,000 / Cr Murabaha payable 2,300,000. Each month: Dr Payable 230,000 / Cr Cash 230,000, and Dr Finance cost 30,000 / Cr Deferred cost 30,000.
The bank buys a machine for KES 1,200,000 and rents it to a clinic for KES 40,000 a month for 5 years.
Dr Ijara asset 1,200,000 / Cr Cash 1,200,000. The bank owns it.
Dr Cash 40,000 / Cr Ijara rental income 40,000.
1,200,000 ÷ 60 months = 20,000. Dr Depreciation 20,000 / Cr Accumulated depreciation 20,000. Bank's monthly margin: 40,000 − 20,000 = 20,000.
Juma gives KES 500,000 to Halima, who runs a shop. They agree to split profit 60% Juma, 40% Halima.
Profit KES 100,000. Juma gets 60,000 and Halima 40,000. Total 100,000.
Loss KES 50,000 with no carelessness. Juma's capital falls to 450,000; Halima loses only her time and effort.

children.topic: Musharaka: two partners in a matatu
children.note: Otieno puts in KES 600,000 and Wanjiru KES 400,000 (60:40). They agree profit 50:50 because Wanjiru runs it.
Shared by the agreed ratio: 100,000 each.
Losses follow capital: Otieno 30,000 (60%), Wanjiru 20,000 (40%). Total 50,000.
Watch for these. Examiners love them.
Murabaha profit and ijara rent are not interest. Use the right account names.

children.topic: Booking all profit on day one
children.note: In an instalment murabaha, profit is deferred and earned over the period, not taken at the sale date.
Extra money from late payers is usually given to charity, not kept as bank income.
In musharaka, profit can follow any agreed ratio, but losses follow capital. In mudaraba, the investor bears money losses unless the manager was at fault.

manas.q: How are losses shared in musharaka?

children.note: If the bank never really holds the item, the deal may not be a true murabaha. Check the paperwork and the order of steps.
Nisab and what counts as zakat wealth vary between scholars. Say so and advise checking with a qualified scholar.
Try each one before opening the steps.
A bank buys a generator for KES 1,500,000 and sells it at a 20% markup over 12 months. Find the price, the instalment and the monthly profit.
300,000 ÷ 12 = KES 25,000. Dr Deferred murabaha profit 25,000 / Cr Murabaha profit income 25,000.
Profit is KES 240,000 and the ratio is 70% investor, 30% manager. Who gets what?
Capital is A KES 800,000 and B KES 400,000. The loss is KES 90,000. Share it.
Capital ratio 2:1. A bears 60,000, B bears 30,000. Total 90,000.
Qualifying wealth after debts is KES 1,200,000 and above nisab. Find zakat at 2.5%.
Kenya has full Islamic banks and conventional banks that offer Islamic products. All banks are licensed by the Central Bank of Kenya.
A Kenyan commercial bank working under an Islamic banking model, licensed by the Central Bank of Kenya.
A Sharia-compliant Kenyan bank, approved in 2007 and opened in 2008 as First Community Bank. It now trades as Premier Bank Kenya.

manas.q: What is First Community Bank's name now?

children.note: Part of the Dubai Islamic Bank group, and listed among Kenya's licensed banks.
Some conventional banks run Islamic 'windows': separate Sharia-compliant accounts and financing inside a normal bank. Their funds and records must be kept apart.

manas.q: What is an Islamic banking window?

children.note: Takaful cover and sukuk are growing in Kenya. Laws and tax rules here keep changing, so check the latest with CBK, the Capital Markets Authority and KRA.

nodeData.note: How a business captures, stores and reports its money data, from paper books to ERP systems. Covers the parts of an AIS, transaction cycles, coding, data flow, controls and Kenyan links like eTIMS and M-Pesa.

children.note: An accounting information system (AIS) is the whole set-up a business uses to capture money events, store them and turn them into reports. It can be a paper cash book or a full computer system.
An AIS collects, stores and processes financial data so that managers, owners, lenders and KRA can make decisions from it.

manas.q: What is an accounting information system (AIS)?

children.note: Without a good system, records are late, wrong or lost. A good AIS gives quick, reliable numbers and makes fraud harder.

children.topic: The six parts of an AIS
children.note: Every AIS, big or small, has the same six building blocks. Remember them as: people, procedures, data, software, IT infrastructure and internal controls.
The users: cashiers, clerks, accountants, managers and auditors who enter, check and use the data.

manas.q: Name the six parts of an AIS.

children.note: The written steps for doing the work, such as how an invoice is raised or who approves a payment.
The facts recorded: customer names, invoice amounts, dates, item codes and tax details.
The programs that record and report, for example QuickBooks, Sage, Odoo or a pharmacy point-of-sale system.
The hardware and networks the software runs on: computers, servers, internet, printers and phones.
The checks that keep data correct and safe, such as passwords, approvals and backups.
A duka owner may use a receipt book and a cash book; a hospital uses an integrated system. Both are an AIS; the computer just makes it faster and links the steps.
Think of the AIS as a machine: input (source documents), processing (journals and ledgers), output (reports like the trial balance and financial statements).

manas.q: What are the three stages of data in an AIS?

children.note: Business events repeat in groups called transaction cycles. Each cycle has its own documents, people and controls.
A transaction cycle is a set of linked steps that happen again and again, like selling and collecting cash.

manas.q: What is a transaction cycle?

children.note: Getting the customer order, delivering goods, sending the invoice and collecting the money.

manas.q: What are the main steps in the revenue cycle?

children.note: Asking for goods, sending a purchase order, receiving goods, checking the supplier invoice and paying.
Keeping staff records, recording hours, working out pay and deductions, paying salaries and remitting deductions.
Planning production, using materials and labour, and costing finished goods. A bakery or a juice maker has one.
Raising money from owners and lenders, repaying loans and paying interest or dividends.
Collecting results from all cycles into the general ledger and producing the trial balance and financial statements.

manas.q: Which cycle produces the financial statements?

children.note: The chart of accounts is the list of every account the business uses, each with a number. Good codes make data easy to sort and report.

children.topic: What a chart of accounts is
children.note: A numbered list of all ledger accounts, grouped into assets, liabilities, equity, income and expenses.

manas.q: What is a chart of accounts?

children.note: A common pattern: 1000s assets, 2000s liabilities, 3000s equity, 4000s income, 5000s and up for expenses. Each business can choose its own.

manas.q: Give a common numbering pattern for a chart of accounts.

children.note: 1100 Bank, 1110 M-Pesa till, 1200 Trade receivables, 1300 Inventory, 2100 Trade payables, 2200 VAT payable, 4000 Sales, 5000 Cost of sales.
Sequence codes (numbers in order), block codes (a range per group) and group codes (each digit means something, such as branch then account).

manas.q: Name three kinds of coding used in an AIS.

children.note: Do not number accounts 1, 2, 3. Leave gaps (1100, 1110, 1120) so new accounts can fit later in the right group.
Customers, suppliers, stock items and staff also get codes. A code is safer than typing a name, which can be spelt many ways.
Software ranges from simple cloud bookkeeping tools to big ERP systems that run the whole business. See the related map "Accounting software".
Enterprise resource planning (ERP) software links all departments (sales, stores, HR, finance) in one system with one shared database.

manas.q: What is an ERP system?

children.topic: The finance module is the core
children.note: In an ERP, the finance module holds the general ledger. Every sale, purchase or payroll run in another module posts to it automatically.
Used by large groups such as banks, manufacturers and telecoms. Powerful but costly to buy, set up and support.
Microsoft Dynamics 365 Business Central and Odoo suit medium firms. Odoo has a free community edition and paid apps.
Small firms often use QuickBooks Online, Xero or Sage. You pay a monthly fee and use it from a browser or phone.
Cloud software runs on the vendor's servers over the internet; on-premise runs on the firm's own computers. Cloud is easier to reach from anywhere but needs reliable internet.

manas.q: What is the difference between cloud and on-premise software?

children.note: Match it to the size of the business, the budget, local support, eTIMS link and M-Pesa features. A matatu owner does not need SAP.
Data flows in a fixed path: document, entry, journal, ledger, trial balance, reports. Each step should leave a trail you can follow back.
The first evidence of a transaction: customer order, delivery note, invoice, receipt, payslip or M-Pesa message.

manas.q: What is a source document?

children.note: The clerk keys in or the system captures the data, for example scanning a barcode at the till.
Transactions are first listed in day books or journals: sales day book, purchases day book, cash book.
Totals are posted to accounts in the general ledger. Customer and supplier details go to sub-ledgers (receivables and payables).
A list of all ledger balances. Total debits must equal total credits, or there is an error to find.

manas.q: What must be true of a trial balance?

children.note: Income statement, statement of financial position, VAT return data and management reports.
You should be able to trace a report figure back to the document, and a document forward to the report.

manas.q: What is an audit trail?

children.note: Follow one sale by Nuru Pharmacy Supplies to a clinic on credit, from order to trial balance. VAT is included at 16% (check the current KRA rate).
Before the sale the trial balance shows: Bank Dr KES 100,000, Inventory Dr KES 80,000, Capital Cr KES 180,000. Debits 180,000 = Credits 180,000.
A clinic orders medicines priced KES 50,000 before VAT. The system checks the clinic's credit limit and creates a sales order. No ledger entry yet.
The stores pick and send the goods, which cost Nuru KES 30,000. The delivery note is signed by the clinic as proof.
Invoice: goods KES 50,000 plus VAT 16% (check the current KRA rate) KES 8,000 = KES 58,000. The invoice is sent through eTIMS so KRA receives it.
Dr Trade receivables 58,000 / Cr Sales 50,000 / Cr VAT payable 8,000. Debits 58,000 = credits 58,000.
Dr Cost of sales 30,000 / Cr Inventory 30,000. The system does this itself when stock leaves the store.
Bank 100,000 Dr; Inventory 50,000 Dr; Receivables 58,000 Dr; Cost of sales 30,000 Dr; Capital 180,000 Cr; Sales 50,000 Cr; VAT payable 8,000 Cr.
The clinic pays KES 58,000 to the paybill. Dr Bank (M-Pesa) 58,000 / Cr Trade receivables 58,000. Receivables go back to nil.
Profit on this sale is sales 50,000 less cost 30,000 = KES 20,000. The VAT of 8,000 is not income; it is owed to KRA.
Controls stop errors and fraud and keep data safe. See the related map "Information security".
Each user gets a login and only the screens they need. A cashier can record sales but cannot change prices or delete invoices.

manas.q: What are access rights in an AIS?

children.note: Split key tasks among different people: one approves, one records, one holds the asset. Then one person alone cannot steal and hide it.

manas.q: What is segregation of duties?

children.note: The system records who entered or changed what and when. Entries are reversed, not deleted, so history is kept.
Copies of data kept safely, ideally one copy off site or in the cloud, and tested by restoring. Protects against theft, fire and ransomware.

manas.q: Why must backups be tested?

children.note: Checks at entry: required fields, valid dates, a customer code that exists, limits on amounts, and totals checked against the documents.

manas.q: Give three examples of input controls.

children.note: Payments, credit notes and new suppliers need a manager's approval in the system before they go through.
Regularly match the books with outside records: bank and M-Pesa statements, supplier statements and the eTIMS sales list.
General controls cover the whole IT set-up (passwords, backups, change control). Application controls sit inside one process (input checks, approvals).

manas.q: What is the difference between general and application controls?

children.note: Kenyan systems must link to KRA and handle M-Pesa. Read the related maps "eTIMS invoicing" and "Computers and information systems".
KRA's electronic Tax Invoice Management System (eTIMS) receives invoices from the seller's system. Many ERPs and POS tools now connect to it directly.

manas.q: What is eTIMS?

children.note: Small traders can use KRA's own eTIMS portal or app; bigger firms link their invoicing or ERP system so each invoice is sent automatically.
Make sure every invoice in the books also appears in eTIMS, and fix any that failed to send. Missing invoices cause tax problems.
Customers pay to a paybill or till number. Each payment has a reference, such as an invoice or account number, so it can be matched.
Download the M-Pesa statement (often as CSV or Excel) and import it into the software, then match each payment to a customer invoice.
iTax is KRA's online portal for filing returns such as VAT and income tax and paying via a payment slip. Data from the AIS feeds these returns.

manas.q: What is iTax used for?

children.note: Lock down KRA PINs and passwords. Only named staff should file returns, and their access should be removed when they leave.
These mistakes cause wrong reports or let fraud slip through. Exams like to test them.
A trusted clerk who orders, receives, records and pays is the classic fraud risk. Always split duties or add a review.
If staff share one login, the audit trail cannot show who did what.
Many firms only learn their backup does not work when the computer is stolen. Test restores regularly.
Wrong entries should be reversed with a new entry, not deleted, so the trail stays complete.
VAT collected is a liability owed to KRA, not sales. Put it in VAT payable.
Too many similar accounts ("Misc", "Other", "Sundry") make reports useless. Keep it short and clear.

children.note: Answer below.

children.topic: Q2: Credit sale KES 20,000 plus VAT
children.note: Use VAT 16% (check the current KRA rate).

children.topic: Q3: Why separate cashier and recorder?
children.note: Answer below.

children.topic: Q4: List the revenue cycle steps
children.note: Answer below.

nodeData.note: How Kenyan SACCOs and co-operatives keep their books: members' deposits and shares, loans and loss provisions, rebates and dividends, reserves and the regulators. Uses an invented SACCO for every example.

children.note: Start here: who owns a SACCO or co-operative, why people join, and why its books look a little different from a normal company's.
A business owned and run by its members, for its members. Each member usually has one vote, however many shares they hold.

manas.q: What is a co-operative?

children.note: A savings and credit co-operative: members save together, and the pooled savings are lent back to members as loans. It is the African name for a credit union.

manas.q: What is a SACCO?

children.note: Dairy, coffee, tea and housing co-operatives are common. They buy from or serve members, and share the surplus back to them.
The same people put in the money, borrow the money and vote on the rules. This is the key idea behind most of the accounting.
Co-ops usually call what is left after costs the surplus. It is shared back to members, kept as reserves or used to grow.
An invented SACCO used in every example below. It serves teachers and small traders; all its numbers are made up for learning.
Members put money in two different pots. Getting this split right is the first big rule of SACCO books.
Money members save regularly, often every month. It earns a yearly interest payment and backs the loans they can take.

manas.q: What are members' deposits in a SACCO?

children.note: The SACCO owes deposits back to the member when they leave, so they sit in liabilities, not equity.

manas.q: Where do members' deposits go on the balance sheet?

children.note: The member's ownership stake. It gives membership and voting rights, earns a dividend, and normally cannot be withdrawn on demand.

manas.q: What is share capital in a SACCO?

children.note: A leaving member usually sells or transfers shares to another member, as the by-laws allow, instead of taking cash from the SACCO.
Members' shares count as equity only if the co-op can refuse to pay them out, or the law or by-laws stop it. If members can demand cash back, they are a liability.

manas.q: What does IFRIC 2 say about members' shares?

children.note: Some SACCOs also run ordinary withdrawable savings accounts at a front office. These are liabilities too, kept separate from members' deposits.
A small one-off fee to join. It is income for the SACCO, not part of the member's savings.

manas.q: How is a SACCO entrance fee recorded?

children.note: Lending is the SACCO's main business. Loans are its biggest asset, and interest on them is its main income.
Money lent to members is owed back to the SACCO, so it is shown as loans to members under assets.

manas.q: Where do loans to members appear?

children.note: Many SACCOs let a member borrow a multiple of their deposits, as their own loan rules say. This is why saving regularly matters.
Other members guarantee a loan with their own deposits. If the borrower fails to pay, the guarantors' deposits can be used.

manas.q: What is a loan guarantor in a SACCO?

children.note: Usually charged on the reducing balance: each month, interest is worked out on what is still owed. It is income for the SACCO.

manas.q: What is reducing-balance interest?

children.note: Each instalment is part interest (income) and part principal (reduces the loan). Record the two parts separately.
Fees charged when a loan is given. Under IFRS 9 they are usually spread over the loan's life as part of the interest, not taken all at once.
Some members will not repay. IFRS 9 Financial Instruments makes the SACCO set money aside for expected losses before they happen.
The amount of loans the SACCO expects it will not collect, weighed by how likely that is. It is booked as a loss allowance.

manas.q: What is expected credit loss (ECL)?

children.note: The older rule waited for a loss to happen. IFRS 9 asks you to look ahead and provide for likely losses now.

manas.q: How is IFRS 9 different from the older incurred-loss approach?

children.note: Loans paid on time with no sign of trouble. Provide for losses expected from defaults in the next 12 months.

manas.q: What is Stage 1 under IFRS 9?

children.note: The borrower is late or credit risk has clearly gone up. Provide for losses over the whole remaining life of the loan.

manas.q: What is Stage 2 under IFRS 9?

children.note: The loan is in real trouble, for example long overdue. Lifetime losses are provided, and interest is based on the net amount.

manas.q: What is Stage 3 under IFRS 9?

children.note: A contra account that sits against loans. Loans minus the allowance gives the net amount the SACCO expects to collect.
When there is no real hope of payment, remove the loan and use up the allowance: Dr Loss allowance / Cr Loans to members.
A licensed SACCO must also follow any provisioning guidance from SASRA. Check the current official guidance; do not guess rates.
At year end members get rewarded in two ways. One is a cost of the SACCO; the other shares out its surplus.
A yearly interest payment on members' deposits. Because deposits are a liability, it is treated as an expense (a finance cost).

manas.q: How is interest on members deposits (rebate) treated?

children.note: A share of the surplus paid on shares. It comes out of equity, not out of expenses.

manas.q: How is a dividend on share capital treated?

children.note: Dividends are proposed by the board and approved by members at the annual general meeting. Record the payable only after approval.
A dairy or coffee co-op may pay back part of the surplus based on how much each member sold through it, not on shares.

manas.q: What is a patronage rebate?

children.note: Members can receive the payment in cash, or have it credited to their deposits or shares if they choose.
Rules protect members' money. Know the reserve that must be kept and who supervises SACCOs.
Part of each year's surplus that the law requires the SACCO to set aside and not share out. It makes the SACCO stronger.

manas.q: What is a statutory reserve?

children.note: It is moved within equity from retained surplus: Dr Retained surplus / Cr Statutory reserve. It is not an expense.
The share of surplus to transfer is set in the law and regulations. Read the current rules on the official SASRA site; do not rely on memory.
The Sacco Societies Regulatory Authority licenses deposit-taking SACCOs and authorises certain non-deposit-taking SACCOs in Kenya.

manas.q: What does SASRA do?

children.note: The Sacco Societies Act of 2008 is the law that created SASRA, which started in 2010 as a body corporate.

manas.q: Which law set up SASRA?

children.note: Deposit-taking SACCOs take withdrawable savings and fall under 2010 regulations. Some non-deposit-taking SACCOs are covered by 2021 regulations.
The Commissioner of Co-operative Development is the government office that oversees co-operatives in general, alongside SASRA for SACCOs.

manas.q: Who oversees co-operatives generally in Kenya?

children.note: The general law for registering and running co-operatives in Kenya. SACCOs follow it plus the Sacco Societies Act.
SACCOs report under IFRS, including IFRS 9 for loans. Smaller co-ops may use IFRS for SMEs; check what the regulator and auditor require.
All figures are for the invented Pamoja Mfano Sacco. Every entry balances: debits equal credits.

Dr Cash 26,000 / Cr Entrance fee income 1,000 / Cr Share capital 20,000 / Cr Members' deposits 5,000. Total debits 26,000 = credits 26,000.
Only the KES 1,000 fee is income. The other KES 25,000 belongs to Wanjiru, as equity (shares) or a liability (deposits).

children.topic: A loan and its first repayment
children.note: Wanjiru borrows KES 300,000 at 1% a month on the reducing balance. Her first instalment is KES 15,000.
Dr Loans to members 300,000 / Cr Cash 300,000.
1% x KES 300,000 = KES 3,000 interest. The rest, 15,000 - 3,000 = KES 12,000, reduces the loan.

Suppose the rule needs KES 470,000. Dr Retained surplus 470,000 / Cr Statutory reserve 470,000.

2,350,000 - 470,000 - 1,500,000 = KES 380,000 stays in retained surplus to grow the SACCO.

10,000 x 50 = KES 500,000. Dr Milk purchases 500,000 / Cr Payable to members 500,000.
10,000 x 60 = KES 600,000. Dr Receivable from processor 600,000 / Cr Sales 600,000. Gross surplus = KES 100,000.
Examiners and auditors look for these slips again and again.
Deposits are owed back to members, so they are liabilities. Only shares the SACCO can refuse to repay are equity.
Dividends on shares come out of equity after AGM approval. The rebate on deposits is the expense.

children.topic: Booking all of a repayment as income
children.note: Only the interest part is income. The principal part just reduces the loan asset.

children.topic: No provision until a loss happens
children.note: IFRS 9 needs a forward-looking allowance from day one, even for good loans (Stage 1).

children.topic: Treating the reserve as a cost
children.note: The statutory reserve transfer is a move inside equity. It does not reduce the surplus figure.
Reserve, liquidity and capital rules change. Quote them only from the current official source.

nodeData.note: How banks and microfinance institutions keep their books. Their 'stock' is money: deposits they owe and loans they are owed. Examples use invented banks and KES figures; this is a general guide only.

children.note: A bank takes in money from savers and lends it to borrowers. It earns more on loans than it pays on deposits, and that gap pays its costs and profit.
Savers leave money with the bank; the bank lends most of it out. This is called financial intermediation.

manas.q: What is financial intermediation?

children.note: Microfinance means small loans, savings and other money services for people with low incomes or no access to normal banks.

manas.q: What is microfinance?

children.note: Commercial banks, microfinance banks, SACCOs, digital lenders and mobile money all serve savers and borrowers, each under different rules.
For a shop, cash is stock to sell. For a bank, money itself is the product, so deposits and loans are the biggest items on its balance sheet.
SACCOs also take members' savings and lend to members. The same ideas here (deposits owed, loans owned, bad-loan allowance) apply to them.
Think from the bank's side, not yours. What the bank owes you is its liability; what you owe the bank is its asset.
Your deposit is money the bank must pay back when you ask. So for the bank it is something it owes (a liability), even though it holds the cash.

manas.q: Why is a customer deposit a liability for the bank?

children.note: A loan is money the borrower must repay with interest. The bank owns that right to be repaid, so it is an asset (loans and advances).

manas.q: Why is a loan an asset for the bank?

children.note: When you deposit, the bank credits your account because its liability to you grows. Your own books show the same money as a debit to your bank asset.
Cash, balances with the Central Bank, government securities (Treasury bills and bonds) and buildings. Loans are usually the largest.
Customer deposits are usually the largest. Banks also owe money borrowed from other banks and lenders.
Share capital plus retained profits. It is the cushion that absorbs losses before depositors are hurt.

manas.q: What is a bank's equity and why does it matter?

children.note: Assets = Liabilities + Equity still holds. Example: assets KES 10,000m = deposits 8,000m + borrowings 800m + equity 1,200m.
Most bank profit comes from interest earned on loans minus interest paid on deposits.
Interest the bank earns on loans, Treasury bills and other lending. It is recorded over time as it is earned, not only when cash comes in.

manas.q: What is interest income for a bank?

children.note: Interest the bank pays to depositors and other lenders. It is a cost recorded as time passes.

manas.q: What is interest expense for a bank?

children.note: Interest income minus interest expense. It is the bank's version of gross profit.

manas.q: What is net interest income?

children.note: Net interest income = interest income − interest expense.
Net interest income divided by average interest-earning assets, shown as a percentage. It shows how well the bank earns on what it lends and invests.

manas.q: What is net interest margin and how is it calculated?

children.note: NIM = net interest income ÷ average earning assets × 100.
Spread is just loan rate minus deposit rate. NIM also reflects how much the bank lends compared with what it borrows, so the two can differ.
Charges for transfers, account keeping, loan processing and cards. These are non-interest income and add to profit.
Under IFRS 9, loan fees that are really part of the interest are spread over the loan's life with the interest, not taken all on day one.

manas.q: How does IFRS 9 treat loan arrangement fees?

children.note: Some borrowers will not repay. IFRS 9 asks banks to set aside an allowance for expected losses before a loan goes bad.
IFRS 9 Financial Instruments is the standard for loans and other financial assets. It replaced IAS 39 from 1 January 2018.

manas.q: Which standard covers bank loan impairment?

children.note: The old way booked a loss only after something went wrong. IFRS 9 books losses the bank reasonably expects, using past data, today's facts and forecasts.

manas.q: What is the expected credit loss (ECL) idea?

children.note: Loans with no big rise in risk since they were given. Allowance = losses expected from defaults in the next 12 months.

manas.q: What is Stage 1 under IFRS 9?

children.note: Credit risk has risen a lot since the loan was given (for example, payments are late). Allowance = losses expected over the whole remaining life.

manas.q: What is Stage 2 under IFRS 9?

children.note: The loan is in real trouble or in default. Allowance is lifetime losses, and interest is worked out on the loan after deducting the allowance.

manas.q: What is Stage 3 under IFRS 9?

children.note: In simple terms: chance of default × amount lost if default happens × amount owed at that time. Banks also weigh several possible futures.

manas.q: What are the three ingredients of ECL?

children.topic: How it shows in the books
children.note: The allowance is deducted from loans on the balance sheet. Increases go to profit or loss as an impairment charge.
When there is no real hope of recovery, the loan and its allowance are both removed. Money recovered later is shown as income.
Two safety ideas regulators watch: does the bank have enough owners' money to take losses, and enough cash to pay depositors on time?
Equity sits between losses and depositors. If loans go bad, the owners lose first.

manas.q: What is bank capital in plain words?

children.note: Capital compared with risk-weighted assets. Riskier assets need more capital behind them. Each regulator sets its own minimums.

manas.q: What is the capital adequacy ratio?

children.note: A bank can be profitable yet fail if many depositors want cash at once and its money is tied up in long loans.

manas.q: What is liquidity risk for a bank?

children.note: Basel III is an international framework from the Basel Committee for bank capital, liquidity and leverage. Countries adapt it into local rules.
ECL charges reduce profit and so reduce capital. Good impairment numbers keep capital figures honest.
Who supervises banks and microfinance in Kenya, plus two Kenyan inventions: mobile money and group lending.
Kenya's monetary authority, based in Nairobi and founded in 1966. It licenses and supervises banks and microfinance banks.

manas.q: Who regulates banks in Kenya?

children.note: The law under which commercial banks and financial institutions are registered and supervised in Kenya.
The law (Cap 493D) under which microfinance banks are licensed and regulated by the CBK.
A 2021 law lets the CBK oversee digital lenders and revoke licences of those that break data-protection or consumer-protection laws.
Launched in 2007 by Safaricom and Vodafone. Users deposit, send, pay and get credit and savings by phone.
The e-money in your M-Pesa account is owed to you, so for the provider it is a liability, like a bank deposit.
An agent holds two assets: cash in the till and e-money float. Serving customers swaps one for the other; commission is the agent's income.
Small borrowers form a group and back each other's loans. Peer pressure and support replace the collateral they do not have.

manas.q: What is microfinance group lending?

children.note: Members meet weekly, save small amounts and repay together. The loan officer collects at the meeting.
Each member's loan is still an asset of the MFI, and group savings it holds are a liability. Group guarantees help when judging expected losses.

Watch out for these. Most come from looking at the bank from the customer's side.
A deposit is not revenue. The bank owes it back, so it is a liability.
Under IFRS 9 you do not wait for a loss event. Stage 1 loans already carry a 12-month allowance.
Stage 1 uses 12-month losses; Stages 2 and 3 use lifetime losses. Mixing these up is a classic exam error.
For credit-impaired loans, work interest on the amount after the allowance.
NIM divides net interest income by earning assets. A rate gap alone is the spread.
If the loan was already provided for, the write-off uses the allowance and is not a second expense.

nodeData.note: How insurers keep their books: premiums earned over time, claims and reserves, reinsurance and agent commission, and IFRS 17 in plain words. A general guide with an invented insurer and figures.

children.note: An insurer collects small regular payments from many people and pays the few who suffer a loss. Its books must show what it has earned so far and what it may still have to pay.
Thousands of car owners each pay a little. Only a few crash in a year, and the pool of money pays for them. That is the basic idea of insurance.

manas.q: What is the basic idea of insurance?

children.note: A written promise: the customer pays, and the insurer agrees to pay if a stated event happens, like a fire, a crash, illness or death.

manas.q: What is an insurance contract (policy)?

children.note: General insurance covers things like cars, buildings and medical bills, usually for one year. Life insurance pays on death or at a set date and can run for many years.

manas.q: What is the difference between general and life insurance?

children.note: The customer pays at the start, but claims arrive later, some years later. This timing gap is why insurance accounting is special.
Insurers earn from cover (premiums higher than claims and costs) and from investing the money they hold until claims are paid.

manas.q: What are the two main sources of an insurer's profit?

children.note: A short list of words you will meet in every insurer's accounts. Learn them before the entries.
The price the customer pays for cover. Money received is not all income at once; it is earned over the period of cover.

manas.q: What is a premium?

children.note: Earned premium is the part for cover already given. Unearned premium is the part for cover still to come, so it is a liability, not income yet.

manas.q: What is unearned premium?

children.note: A request by a customer to be paid for a loss the policy covers. Once a loss happens, the insurer owes money even if it has not yet paid.

manas.q: What is a claim?

children.note: Claims that have been reported to the insurer but not yet fully paid. The insurer records its best estimate as a liability.

manas.q: What are outstanding claims?

children.note: Incurred but not reported: losses that have already happened but the customer has not told the insurer yet. Actuaries estimate them, and they are a liability too.

manas.q: What does IBNR mean?

children.note: The cost of claims belonging to this year: claims paid, plus closing outstanding claims, minus opening outstanding claims.

manas.q: What is the formula for claims incurred?

children.note: Money the insurer must hold for future claims and cover it still owes. The accounts call these insurance contract liabilities; people often say reserves.

manas.q: Why does an insurer hold reserves?

children.note: A specialist in risk and statistics who estimates future claims and how much the insurer must hold. Accountants use these estimates in the books.
Besides premiums and claims, insurers pay agents, buy their own cover and invest. Each needs correct entries.
Agents and brokers who sell policies earn a commission, often a percentage of the premium. It is a cost of getting the business (acquisition cost).

manas.q: What is an insurance acquisition cost?

children.note: The insurer passes part of its risk to a reinsurer and pays it a share of premium. If a big claim comes, the reinsurer pays its part back.

manas.q: What is reinsurance?

children.note: The reinsurer takes a fixed percentage of every policy, both premiums and claims. Example: 40% of premium and 40% of each claim.
The reinsurer pays only the part of a loss above an agreed amount, for example any part of one claim above KES 5 million.
The insurer still owes its customer the full claim. The amount due back from the reinsurer is shown as a separate asset, not netted off.
Premiums are invested in things like government bonds and deposits until claims are paid. The return is investment income, shown apart from insurance results.
IFRS 17 Insurance Contracts is the world standard for insurers' books. It replaced the old interim standard IFRS 4 and took effect on 1 January 2023.
Under IFRS 4 insurers in different countries used very different methods, so accounts were hard to compare. IFRS 17 gives one common approach.

manas.q: Which standard did IFRS 17 replace, and from when?

children.note: Similar contracts are put in groups, and a group cannot mix contracts issued more than one year apart. Each group is measured together.
Estimate future cash in and out, adjust for the time value of money (discounting), and add a cushion for uncertainty (risk adjustment).

manas.q: What are the building blocks of IFRS 17 measurement?

children.note: The profit the insurer expects to earn but has not yet earned. It sits in the liability and is released to income as cover is given.

manas.q: What is the contractual service margin (CSM)?

children.note: If a group is expected to lose money, the whole expected loss is shown at once. There is no CSM to spread.

manas.q: When is an insurance contract onerous, and what happens?

children.note: The premium allocation approach is a simpler method, mainly for short cover of a year or less. It works much like the old unearned premium idea.

manas.q: What is the premium allocation approach (PAA)?

children.note: A version for contracts where the customer shares in the returns of investments the insurer holds, such as some life savings policies.
Insurance revenue is earned as cover is given, and any savings part the customer will get back anyway is left out of revenue.

children.topic: Two results in profit or loss
children.note: The insurance service result shows profit from cover. The finance result shows investment income less the interest effect on the liabilities.
An invented insurer, Simba Cover Insurance Ltd, year end 31 December. All figures are made up for learning.
A one-year motor policy starts 1 October for KES 120,000, paid in cash. By 31 December, 3 months of cover is given.
Dr Bank 120,000 / Cr Unearned premium (liability) 120,000. No income yet, because no cover has been given.
120,000 x 3/12 = 30,000 earned. Dr Unearned premium 30,000 / Cr Insurance revenue 30,000.
Unearned premium at 31 December = 120,000 - 30,000 = KES 90,000, a liability for the 9 months still to come.
In November a customer crashes. The estimate is KES 200,000. Simba pays KES 150,000 in December.
Dr Claims expense 200,000 / Cr Outstanding claims (liability) 200,000.
Dr Outstanding claims 150,000 / Cr Bank 150,000. Still owed at year end: 200,000 - 150,000 = KES 50,000.
The actuary estimates KES 40,000 of accidents happened before 31 December but are not yet reported. Dr Claims expense 40,000 / Cr IBNR liability 40,000.
The agent earns 10% of 120,000 = KES 12,000. Dr Acquisition costs 12,000 / Cr Bank 12,000. Under PAA for one-year cover, Simba may expense it at once.
If Simba spreads it instead: 3/12 x 12,000 = 3,000 expense this year, and 9,000 stays in the balance sheet against the liability, released next year.
Simba gives a reinsurer 40% of the policy. Premium ceded: 40% x 120,000 = KES 48,000. Dr Reinsurance premium 48,000 / Cr Payable to reinsurer 48,000.
40% x 200,000 = 80,000. Dr Reinsurance recoverable (asset) 80,000 / Cr Reinsurance recoveries 80,000.

children.topic: Simba's net cost of the claim
children.note: Gross claim 200,000 - recovery 80,000 = KES 120,000 net cost. The full 200,000 still shows as a liability to the customer.

children.topic: All premium as income on day one
children.note: Only the earned part is income. The rest is unearned premium, a liability.
Losses that happened but were not reported still belong to this year. Leaving them out overstates profit.

children.topic: Claims paid is not claims incurred
children.note: Claims incurred = paid + closing outstanding - opening outstanding. Using only cash paid is wrong.

manas.q: Why is claims paid not the same as claims incurred?

children.note: The insurer owes the full claim to the customer. Show what the reinsurer owes back as a separate asset.
IFRS 17 applies from 1 January 2023. Answers about current accounts should use IFRS 17 words like CSM and insurance revenue.
An onerous group's expected loss is shown at once, not spread over time.

children.topic: Q1: A one-year policy of KES 240,000

Claims paid in the year KES 300,000; outstanding claims at start KES 80,000; at end KES 120,000.

children.topic: Q3: 30% quota share on a claim

In two sentences, explain the contractual service margin.
It is the profit the insurer expects from a group of contracts but has not yet earned. It is held in the liability and released to revenue as cover is given.
Two special kinds of cover. Learn the main idea of each.
Members pay contributions into a shared fund that helps members who suffer a loss. It avoids interest and excessive uncertainty, so it fits Sharia.

manas.q: What is takaful?

children.note: A company runs the fund for the members and earns a fee or a share of profit. Its own money is kept apart from the members' fund.
Show the members' fund and the operator's own accounts separately. Any surplus in the fund may go back to members.
Cheap, simple cover for people on low incomes, with small premiums for risks like hospital bills, crop loss or funerals.

manas.q: What is micro-insurance?

children.note: Many tiny premiums, often paid by mobile money, so the same rules apply but systems must handle huge numbers of small entries.
How insurers are supervised in Kenya. Check current rules with the regulator before relying on them.
The body that regulates and supervises insurers, reinsurers, agents and brokers in Kenya, and protects policyholders.

manas.q: Who regulates insurance in Kenya?

children.note: The main Kenyan law on insurance. It sets up the IRA and the rules insurers must follow.

manas.q: Which law sets up Kenya's insurance regulator?

children.note: Insurers send regular returns to the IRA, as well as publishing IFRS accounts. Figures and deadlines change, so check the IRA's current rules.
A duka owner buys stock cover and pays KES 30,000 a year. To her it is a prepaid expense; to the insurer it is unearned premium. Same deal, two sides.

nodeData.note: How farms and agribusinesses keep their books: simple records for a small farm, cost per litre or per bag, the IAS 41 rules for living animals and plants, cooperatives like KTDA and dairy co-ops, and grants. All farm names and figures are invented.

children.topic: What it is and why it matters
children.note: Farm accounting tracks money and living things: cows, crops in the field, chickens, tea bushes. It shows the farmer what pays and helps lenders, co-ops and owners trust the numbers.
A farm buys inputs (seed, feed, fertiliser, labour), grows or raises something, and sells it. Like a duka, it needs records to know if it makes a profit.
The main assets are alive. Calves grow, crops ripen and hens age, so their value changes even when nothing is bought or sold.
The farmer, a bank or SACCO giving a loan, the cooperative buying produce, partners in a family farm, and for big agribusinesses, shareholders and auditors.
A smallholder with two cows mostly needs a cash book and simple enterprise records. A large tea or flower company reports under full IFRS, including IAS 41.

children.topic: Simple records for a small farm
children.note: Start simple: write down every shilling in and out, and keep separate records for each farm activity (each 'enterprise').
A book or phone sheet with the date, what it was for, money in and money out, and the balance. Include M-Pesa payments as well as cash.

manas.q: What is a farm cash book?

children.note: Keep income and costs separately for each activity: dairy, maize, poultry. Then you can see which one makes money and which one loses.

manas.q: What are enterprise records on a farm?

children.note: Litres milked per cow each day, litres sold and to whom, feed bought, vet and AI (artificial insemination) costs, and calving dates.
Acres planted, seed and fertiliser used, ploughing and labour costs, bags harvested, bags sold, bags kept for the family.
Number of birds, deaths, eggs collected per day, trays sold, feed bags used, and vaccines given.
A list of animals (with ear tag or name), equipment like a chaff cutter or water tank, and stores of feed and fertiliser. Count them at least once a year.
Milk, eggs or maize eaten by the family are part of what the farm produced. Record them so the true output is not understated.

children.topic: Cost per litre, bag or tray
children.note: Divide the total cost of an enterprise by the amount it produced. Compare this with the selling price to see the margin on each unit.
Unit cost = total costs of the enterprise ÷ units produced. Examples: cost per litre of milk, per 90 kg bag of maize, per tray of 30 eggs.

manas.q: How do you work out cost per litre or per bag?

children.note: Costs that rise with output, such as feed, seed, fertiliser, vaccines and casual labour.

manas.q: What is a variable cost on a farm?

children.note: Costs that stay about the same whatever you produce, such as a permanent worker's wage, land rent or depreciation of a water tank.
Gross margin = income of the enterprise − its variable costs. It is the usual quick way to compare dairy against maize or poultry.

manas.q: What is a gross margin in farm accounting?

children.note: If cost per litre is above the price the co-op pays, change something: better feed, fewer unproductive cows, or a better buyer.
IAS 41 Agriculture is the IFRS standard for farming activity. It says how to value living animals and plants, and farm produce at the moment of harvest.
Managing the growth of animals or plants so they can be sold, harvested or turned into more animals or plants. A dairy farm, a maize farm and a fish pond all count.

manas.q: What is agricultural activity under IAS 41?

children.note: A living animal or plant the farm controls: dairy cows, goats, broilers, layers, maize growing in the field, fish in a pond.

manas.q: What is a biological asset?

children.note: What is harvested from a biological asset: milk from a cow, eggs from a hen, maize cobs from the plant, green tea leaf from the bush.

manas.q: What is agricultural produce?

children.topic: Fair value less costs to sell
children.note: Biological assets are usually measured at fair value (what the market would pay) minus the costs of selling, such as transport to market and auction fees.

manas.q: How does IAS 41 usually measure biological assets?

children.note: When the value of the herd or crop goes up or down between two dates, the gain or loss goes to profit or loss for that period.
Produce is measured at fair value less costs to sell at the point of harvest. After that it is inventory under IAS 2, and that value becomes its cost.

manas.q: What happens to agricultural produce after harvest?

children.note: If there is no reliable market price for a biological asset when it is first recorded, it can be carried at cost less depreciation and impairment until a price is available.
Turning produce into something else, like milk into yoghurt or green leaf into made tea, is not covered by IAS 41. Those products follow IAS 2 Inventories.
Smaller Kenyan entities using IFRS for SMEs have a simpler agriculture section: fair value where it is easy to get without undue cost or effort, otherwise cost.

children.topic: Bearer plants: tea bushes under IAS 16
children.note: Some plants are kept only to produce crops year after year. These bearer plants are treated like machinery under IAS 16 Property, Plant and Equipment.
A living plant used to grow produce for more than one period, and unlikely to be sold as produce itself. Tea bushes, coffee trees, avocado and mango trees are examples.

manas.q: What is a bearer plant?

children.note: Bearer plants follow IAS 16: record the cost of planting and growing them until mature, then depreciate over their useful life.

manas.q: Which standard covers bearer plants such as tea bushes?

children.note: The tea leaf or coffee cherry growing on the plant is still a biological asset under IAS 41 until it is picked.
A dairy cow gives milk for years, but it is an animal, so it stays under IAS 41 at fair value less costs to sell.

manas.q: Is a dairy cow a bearer plant?

children.note: The land under the crop is ordinary property under IAS 16. It is not a biological asset and is not depreciated.
Farm income arrives in lumps at harvest, while costs run all year. Many Kenyan farmers sell through cooperatives, which changes how they are paid and how they record it.
Maize money comes after harvest, but seed and fertiliser are paid months before. Record costs in the season they belong to and plan cash so the farm survives the gap.

manas.q: Why does seasonality matter in farm accounting?

children.note: Bags of maize kept to sell later when prices rise are inventory. Count and value them at the year end.

The Kenya Tea Development Agency serves hundreds of thousands of small tea farmers. Farmers deliver green leaf to its factories and receive regular payments per kilo, with any later bonus paid separately.

manas.q: What is KTDA?

children.note: Farmers deliver milk to a dairy cooperative society, which collects, chills and sells it. The farmer is paid for litres delivered, usually monthly.
Co-ops often deduct feed bought on credit at the co-op store, loan repayments to the linked SACCO, or other agreed charges before paying the farmer.

children.topic: Record the gross, not the net
children.note: Book the full value of produce as sales, then record each deduction as what it really is (an expense or a loan repayment). Do not just record the net cash.
IAS 20 Accounting for Government Grants and Disclosure of Government Assistance covers money or help from government, for example a county grant for a milk cooler.
Grant income is recognised over the periods when the related costs are recognised, not all on the day the cash arrives.

manas.q: When is a government grant recognised as income under IAS 20?

children.note: A grant for equipment can be shown as deferred income released over the asset's life, or deducted from the asset's cost. Either way the yearly charge is reduced.
If a grant relates to a biological asset carried at fair value less costs to sell, IAS 41 has its own rule: an unconditional grant goes to profit when it becomes receivable.
Invented farms, real arithmetic. Check that every set of debits equals the credits.

children.topic: Dairy: cost per litre at Shamba Bora
children.note: Shamba Bora Farm sold 3,000 litres in a month at KES 50 a litre.
3,000 litres × KES 50 = KES 150,000.
Feed 60,000 + vet 8,000 + labour 22,000 + AI and other 5,000 = KES 95,000.
95,000 ÷ 3,000 = about KES 31.67 a litre. The margin is about KES 18.33 a litre.
150,000 − 95,000 = KES 55,000 for the dairy enterprise.
Mama Wanjiku plants 4 acres and harvests 80 bags of 90 kg.
Seed 24,000 + fertiliser 48,000 + ploughing 16,000 + labour 30,000 + shelling and bags 10,000 = KES 128,000.
She sells all 80 bags at KES 3,500: income 280,000. Margin 280,000 − 128,000 = KES 152,000.
Kuku Poa layers produce 12,000 eggs a month, which is 400 trays of 30.
Feed 90,000 + vaccines 4,000 + labour 15,000 + other 3,000 = KES 112,000.
112,000 ÷ 400 = KES 280 a tray. Selling at KES 380 gives 400 × 380 = 152,000 and a margin of KES 40,000.

children.topic: IAS 41: a heifer herd gains value
children.note: Green Hills Agri Ltd owns 20 heifers. Costs to sell are KES 2,000 a head.
Gain 1,360,000 − 1,160,000 = 200,000. Dr Biological assets 200,000 / Cr Gain on biological assets (profit or loss) 200,000.
Milima Estates plucks 10,000 kg of green leaf. Fair value is KES 25 a kg and costs to sell KES 1 a kg.
10,000 × (25 − 1) = 240,000. Dr Inventory (green leaf) 240,000 / Cr Gain on harvested produce 240,000.
Sold at KES 25 a kg: Dr Receivable 250,000 / Cr Revenue 250,000. Then Dr Cost of sales 240,000 / Cr Inventory 240,000. Transport is paid and expensed separately.
Milima Estates spent KES 900,000 planting and raising new tea bushes. They are expected to produce for 30 years.
900,000 ÷ 30 = 30,000. Dr Depreciation expense 30,000 / Cr Accumulated depreciation 30,000.
Baraka delivered 600 litres at KES 48. The co-op deducted KES 6,000 for feed and KES 5,000 SACCO loan repayment.
Dr Bank 17,800 / Dr Feed expense 6,000 / Dr SACCO loan 5,000 / Cr Milk sales 28,800. Debits 28,800 = credits 28,800.
A dairy co-op buys a cooler for KES 900,000 (10-year life) and gets a KES 300,000 county grant for it.
Dr Bank 300,000 / Cr Deferred grant income 300,000.
Dr Depreciation 90,000 / Cr Accumulated depreciation 90,000. Dr Deferred grant income 30,000 / Cr Grant income 30,000. Net cost to profit 60,000 a year.
These slips cost marks and mislead farmers.
School fees paid from milk money are drawings, not farm costs. Keep them out of the enterprise records.
Under IAS 41 take off selling costs. Using the full market price overstates the herd or crop.
Tea bushes are bearer plants under IAS 16. Only the leaf growing on them is IAS 41.

manas.q: Exam trap: are tea bushes measured at fair value?

children.note: After harvest and processing, made tea, yoghurt or maize flour are IAS 2 inventory, not biological assets.
Recording only the cash received hides sales and costs. Book gross sales and each deduction.
Not recording milk drunk at home or birds that died makes unit costs and margins wrong.
Try each one before opening the steps.
A farmer spends KES 150,000 on a maize plot and harvests 60 bags. Find the cost per bag and the margin if each bag sells for KES 3,200.
A farm has 50 goats. Opening fair value KES 8,000 each, closing KES 9,000 each; costs to sell KES 500 each at both dates. Find the gain.
Gain 50,000. Dr Biological assets 50,000 / Cr Gain on biological assets 50,000.
Classify: a tea bush, a dairy cow, tea leaf on the bush, plucked leaf in the store.
Tea bush: IAS 16. Dairy cow: IAS 41. Leaf on the bush: IAS 41. Plucked leaf after harvest: IAS 2 inventory.
A KES 200,000 grant is received for a spray pump with a 5-year life. How much grant income each year?
200,000 ÷ 5 = KES 40,000 a year. Dr Deferred grant income 40,000 / Cr Grant income 40,000.
