nodeData.note: How private hospitals and clinics keep their books: income by department, many payers, insurer and SHA claims, drug stock, costly machines and patient privacy. Uses an invented clinic and figures.

children.topic: What it is and why it matters
children.note: A hospital sells many small services every day and is paid by many different payers. Good books show which departments earn money, who still owes, and what stock is on the shelves.
Hospital accounting is ordinary accounting applied to a business that treats patients. The same double entry works; the hard parts are many payers, claims and drugs that expire.

manas.q: What makes hospital accounting different from a normal shop?

children.note: Mfano Clinic is an invented private clinic in Nairobi with a lab, pharmacy, X-ray room and 20 beds. All its figures here are made up for learning.
Owners and doctors who run it, banks that lend for equipment, KRA, insurers checking claims, and auditors at year end.
Many clinics treat lots of patients yet run short of cash, because insurers pay late or reject claims. Clear books spot this early.
Revenue is tracked by department so managers see which services pay their way. Each department gets its own income account.
What patients pay to see a doctor or specialist. Usually a fixed fee per visit, booked the day the patient is seen.

manas.q: What is consultation revenue?

children.note: Fees for blood tests, malaria tests, urine tests and so on. Often the biggest earner after pharmacy in an outpatient clinic.
Medicines sold to patients, both walk-in and on prescription. This is sales of goods, so it has a matching cost of sales from inventory.

manas.q: Why does pharmacy revenue need a cost of sales figure?

children.note: Fees for imaging scans. The machines are costly, so this department carries heavy depreciation.
Bed days, nursing, theatre and meals for admitted patients. The bill builds up day by day until discharge.
Set up accounts like 'Revenue – Lab' and 'Revenue – Pharmacy'. Then the income statement can show each department's share and margin.

children.topic: Who pays: the three payer types
children.note: The patient gets the service, but the bill is often paid by someone else. Each payer type is handled differently in the books.
Patients who pay themselves by cash, card or M-Pesa at the counter. Money comes in the same day, so there is little or no receivable.

manas.q: What is a cash patient?

children.note: Patients covered by a private medical insurer. The clinic sends a claim and waits to be paid, so it records a receivable from the insurer.

manas.q: Who owes the clinic for an insured patient?

children.note: Patients covered by the Social Health Authority (SHA), the state body that replaced NHIF and began work in October 2024. The clinic claims from SHA's funds, such as the Social Health Insurance Fund (SHIF).

manas.q: Which body replaced NHIF in Kenya?

children.note: Staff of companies that have a credit account with the clinic. The company is billed monthly and pays within agreed terms, for example 30 days.
Part of a bill the insurer will not cover, which the patient pays. Collect it at the counter before the patient leaves.
The insurer's approval before a costly service like admission or a scan. Without it, the claim may be rejected.
Use a separate receivable account for each insurer, for SHA and for each corporate client. Then you can see exactly who owes what and for how long.

manas.q: Why keep a separate receivable for each payer?

children.note: A few accounting standards cover most hospital transactions. Learn the idea behind each one in plain words.
IFRS 15 Revenue from Contracts with Customers says: record income when you deliver the service, at the amount you expect to be paid. Not when cash arrives.

manas.q: When does IFRS 15 say a clinic records revenue?

children.note: 1 Find the contract. 2 Find what you promised. 3 Set the price. 4 Share the price over the promises. 5 Record revenue as each promise is delivered.

manas.q: What are the five steps of IFRS 15?

children.note: A consultation or lab test is delivered on the day, so revenue is booked that day.
Ward care is delivered over time, so revenue builds up each day the patient stays, even before the final bill.
If you expect an insurer to pay less than billed, record only what you expect to receive. A patient who later cannot pay is a bad debt instead.
A deposit taken on admission is money held for services not yet given. It is a liability (owed to the patient) until the care is delivered.

manas.q: Why is a patient deposit a liability, not revenue?

children.note: Drugs and supplies are valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value (what you can sell for, less selling costs).

manas.q: How does IAS 2 value inventory?

children.note: IAS 16 Property, Plant and Equipment: record machines at cost, including delivery and installation, then spread that cost over their useful life by depreciation.

manas.q: What goes into the cost of an X-ray machine under IAS 16?

children.note: Many small Kenyan clinics use IFRS for SMEs, a simpler version. The ideas on revenue, stock and equipment are much the same.
Money owed by insurers, SHA and corporates is checked at year end. Amounts unlikely to be paid are reduced by an allowance for credit losses (IFRS 9).
Drugs expire and machines wear out. Both must be tracked closely or profit will be overstated.
Stock includes medicines, gloves, syringes, lab reagents and X-ray film. Count it regularly and match counts to the system.

manas.q: What counts as medical-supplies inventory?

children.note: Issue the batch that expires soonest first, even if it arrived later. This cuts waste from expired drugs.

manas.q: What does FEFO mean?

children.note: FIFO issues the oldest delivery first. FEFO looks at expiry dates instead. For costing, the books can still use FIFO or weighted average.
Remove expired drugs from saleable stock and write them off as an expense. Dispose of them safely and keep the disposal record.
Spread the cost of X-ray, ultrasound and lab machines over their useful life. Straight line means the same charge each year.

manas.q: What is the straight-line depreciation formula?

children.note: Add up a department's costs for a period and divide by the number of patients or tests. It shows whether the price covers the cost.

manas.q: How do you work out cost per test?

children.note: Direct costs belong to one department, like lab reagents. Shared costs, like rent and power, are spread over departments on a fair basis such as floor space.
Insurer and SHA money comes only after a claim is approved. Managing claims well is how a clinic keeps cash flowing.
Register patient, check cover, get pre-authorisation, treat, bill, send claim, follow up, receive payment, match it to the invoice.
Missing pre-authorisation, wrong member number, service not covered, limit used up, or late submission.
When an insurer refuses part or all of a claim. The clinic either bills the patient, appeals, or writes the amount off.

manas.q: What can a clinic do with a rejected claim?

children.note: Removing an amount you will never collect from receivables and charging it as an expense. It needs a manager's approval.

manas.q: What is a write-off?

children.note: List what each payer owes by age: 0–30, 31–60, 61–90 and over 90 days. Old balances need chasing first.

manas.q: What is a receivables ageing report?

children.note: When an insurer pays, it sends a list of claims paid. Match each line to your invoices so short payments are spotted.
Mfano Clinic's invented figures, in KES. Every entry balances: total debits equal total credits.
Revenue: consultation 45,000; lab 60,000; pharmacy 120,000; radiology 35,000; inpatient 140,000. Total 400,000.
Cash and M-Pesa 150,000; insurers 180,000; SHA 50,000; corporates 20,000. Total 400,000, the same as revenue.
Dr Cash 150,000; Dr Insurer receivables 180,000; Dr SHA receivable 50,000; Dr Corporate receivables 20,000 / Cr each department's revenue as above. Both sides 400,000.
Mr A (invented) is admitted and pays a KES 30,000 deposit. His final bill is 85,000.
Dr Cash 30,000 / Cr Patient deposits (liability) 30,000. No revenue yet.
Dr Patient receivable 85,000 / Cr Inpatient revenue 85,000, built up over his stay.
Dr Patient deposits 30,000 / Cr Patient receivable 30,000. He pays the balance: Dr Cash 55,000 / Cr Patient receivable 55,000. Receivable now nil.
Mfano claims 48,000 from an insurer. It pays 42,000 and rejects 6,000: 2,000 is an excluded item the patient must pay, 4,000 cannot be recovered.
Dr Bank 42,000; Dr Patient receivable 2,000; Dr Claims written off (expense) 4,000 / Cr Insurer receivable 48,000. 42,000 + 2,000 + 4,000 = 48,000.
At year end, drugs costing 18,000 have expired. Another batch cost 50,000 but, near expiry, can sell for only 35,000 less 1,000 costs.
Dr Expired stock expense 18,000 / Cr Inventory 18,000.
Price 3,600,000 plus installation 200,000 = cost 3,800,000. Residual value 300,000, life 7 years.
(3,800,000 − 300,000) ÷ 7 = 500,000 a year. Dr Depreciation expense 500,000 / Cr Accumulated depreciation 500,000.
One month: reagents 180,000; staff 220,000; machine depreciation 40,000; share of rent and power 60,000. Total 500,000 for 2,500 tests.
500,000 ÷ 2,500 = KES 200 per test. If the average price is 450, each test leaves 250 towards profit.
These errors make a clinic look richer than it is, or hide cash problems.
A deposit is not earned until care is given. Booking it as revenue overstates income and hides a liability.

children.topic: Waiting for cash to book revenue
children.note: Insurer work is income when the service is given, not when the insurer finally pays. That is cash accounting, not IFRS 15.
Leaving expired drugs in stock overstates assets and profit. Check expiry dates at every count.
Delivery and installation of a machine are part of its cost under IAS 16, not an expense.
Lumping all insurers together hides which payer is slow or rejecting claims.
Finance reports need amounts and invoice numbers, not diagnoses. Leaking health details is a serious breach.
Finance staff see bills that hint at a patient's illness. That information must be protected like a medical record.
Kenya's Data Protection Act 2019 treats health data as sensitive personal data. Collect only what you need and guard it.

manas.q: How does Kenya's Data Protection Act treat health data?

children.note: In reports and ledgers, use patient or invoice numbers. Keep names and diagnoses in the medical system.
Only staff who must see a bill or claim should be able to open it. Give each user their own login.
Send claim details only through the insurer's or SHA's approved channels, never on open chat groups or personal email.
Teaching examples, like this map, use invented clinics and figures, never a real hospital's data or patient details.

Cost 2,400,000, residual 400,000, life 5 years, straight line. Find the yearly charge and value after 2 years.
After 2 years: 2,400,000 − 800,000 = carrying amount KES 1,600,000.
Claim 30,000; insurer pays 26,500 and the rest cannot be recovered. Write the entry.
Shortfall 3,500. Dr Bank 26,500; Dr Claims written off 3,500 / Cr Insurer receivable 30,000.
Stock cost 12,000; it can now sell for 9,500 with 500 selling costs. Value it under IAS 2.
NRV = 9,500 − 500 = 9,000, below cost. Carry at 9,000 and write down 3,000.
